iris_left.description: In humans and most mammals and birds, the iris (plural: irides or irises) is a thin, annular structure in the eye, responsible for controlling the diameter and size of the pupil, thus the amount of light reaching the retina. Eye color is defined by that of the iris.

iris_right.name: Iris (right)
iris_right.description: In humans and most mammals and birds, the iris (plural: irides or irises) is a thin, annular structure in the eye, responsible for controlling the diameter and size of the pupil, thus the amount of light reaching the retina. Eye color is defined by that of the iris.

jugulodigastric_node_left.name: Jugulodigastric node (left)
jugulodigastric_node_left.description: The jugulodigastric lymph nodes are large lymph nodes of the neck.

jugulodigastric_node_right.name: Jugulodigastric node (right)
jugulodigastric_node_right.description: The jugulodigastric lymph nodes are large lymph nodes of the neck.

labial_commissure_left.name: Labial commissure (left)
labial_commissure_left.description: The commissure is the corner of the mouth, where the vermillion border of the superior labium (upper lip) meets that of the inferior labium (lower lip). The commissure is important in facial appearance, particularly during some functions, including smiling. As such it is of interest to dental surgeons.

labial_commissure_right.name: Labial commissure (right)
labial_commissure_right.description: The commissure is the corner of the mouth, where the vermillion border of the superior labium (upper lip) meets that of the inferior labium (lower lip). The commissure is important in facial appearance, particularly during some functions, including smiling. As such it is of interest to dental surgeons.

lacrimal_artery_left.name: Lacrimal artery (left)
lacrimal_artery_left.description: The lacrimal artery is an artery of the orbit around the eye. It arises close to the optic foramen, and is a branch of the ophthalmic artery. It accompanies the lacrimal nerve along the upper border of the lateral rectus muscle. It supplies the lacrimal gland, two rectus muscles of the eye, the eyelids, and the conjunctiva.

lacrimal_artery_right.name: Lacrimal artery (right)
lacrimal_artery_right.description: The lacrimal artery is an artery of the orbit around the eye. It arises close to the optic foramen, and is a branch of the ophthalmic artery. It accompanies the lacrimal nerve along the upper border of the lateral rectus muscle. It supplies the lacrimal gland, two rectus muscles of the eye, the eyelids, and the conjunctiva.

lacrimal_bone_left.name: Lacrimal bone (left)
lacrimal_bone_left.description: The lacrimal bone is a small and fragile bone of the facial skeleton; it is roughly the size of the little fingernail. It is situated at the front part of the medial wall of the orbit. It has two surfaces and four borders. Several bony landmarks of the lacrimal bone function in the process of lacrimation or crying.

lacrimal_bone_right.name: Lacrimal bone (right)
lacrimal_bone_right.description: The lacrimal bone is a small and fragile bone of the facial skeleton; it is roughly the size of the little fingernail. It is situated at the front part of the medial wall of the orbit. It has two surfaces and four borders. Several bony landmarks of the lacrimal bone function in the process of lacrimation or crying.

lacrimal_canaliculus_left.name: Lacrimal canaliculus (left)
lacrimal_canaliculus_left.description: The lacrimal canaliculi, (sing. canaliculus), are the small channels in each eyelid that drain lacrimal fluid, from the lacrimal puncta to the lacrimal sac. This forms part of the lacrimal apparatus that drains lacrimal fluid from the surface of the eye to the nasal cavity.

lacrimal_canaliculus_right.name: Lacrimal canaliculus (right)
lacrimal_canaliculus_right.description: The lacrimal canaliculi, (sing. canaliculus), are the small channels in each eyelid that drain lacrimal fluid, from the lacrimal puncta to the lacrimal sac. This forms part of the lacrimal apparatus that drains lacrimal fluid from the surface of the eye to the nasal cavity.

lacrimal_gland_left.name: Lacrimal gland (left)
lacrimal_gland_left.description: The lacrimal glands are paired exocrine glands, one for each eye, found in most terrestrial vertebrates and some marine mammals, that secrete the aqueous layer of the tear film. In humans, they are situated in the upper lateral region of each orbit, in the lacrimal fossa of the orbit formed by the frontal bone.

lacrimal_gland_right.name: Lacrimal gland (right)
lacrimal_gland_right.description: The lacrimal glands are paired exocrine glands, one for each eye, found in most terrestrial vertebrates and some marine mammals, that secrete the aqueous layer of the tear film. In humans, they are situated in the upper lateral region of each orbit, in the lacrimal fossa of the orbit formed by the frontal bone.

lacrimal_sac_left.name: Lacrimal sac (left)
lacrimal_sac_left.description: The lacrimal sac or lachrymal sac is the upper dilated end of the nasolacrimal duct, and is lodged in a deep groove formed by the lacrimal bone and frontal process of the maxilla. It connects the lacrimal canaliculi, which drain tears from the eye's surface, and the nasolacrimal duct, which conveys this fluid into the nasal cavity.

lacrimal_sac_right.name: Lacrimal sac (right)
lacrimal_sac_right.description: The lacrimal sac or lachrymal sac is the upper dilated end of the nasolacrimal duct, and is lodged in a deep groove formed by the lacrimal bone and frontal process of the maxilla. It connects the lacrimal canaliculi, which drain tears from the eye's surface, and the nasolacrimal duct, which conveys this fluid into the nasal cavity.

laryngopharynx.name: Laryngopharynx
laryngopharynx.description: The laryngopharynx, (Latin: pars laryngea pharyngis), also known as hypopharynx, is the caudal part of the pharynx; it is the part of the throat that connects to the esophagus.

lateral_geniculate_body_left.name: Lateral geniculate body (left)
lateral_geniculate_body_left.description: The lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN; also called the lateral geniculate body or lateral geniculate complex) is a relay center in the thalamus for the visual pathway. It is a small, ovoid, ventral projection of the thalamus where the thalamus connects with the optic nerve.

lateral_geniculate_body_right.name: Lateral geniculate body (right)
lateral_geniculate_body_right.description: The lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN; also called the lateral geniculate body or lateral geniculate complex) is a relay center in the thalamus for the visual pathway. It is a small, ovoid, ventral projection of the thalamus where the thalamus connects with the optic nerve.

lateral_occipital_artery_left.name: Lateral occipital artery (left)
lateral_occipital_artery_left.description: Lateral terminal branch of the posterior cerebral artery. It is distributed to the basal surface of the occipital lobe and to the posterior part of the temporal lobe. Feneis 248.14

lateral_occipital_artery_right.name: Lateral occipital artery (right)
lateral_occipital_artery_right.description: Lateral terminal branch of the posterior cerebral artery. It is distributed to the basal surface of the occipital lobe and to the posterior part of the temporal lobe. Feneis 248.14

lateral_occipital_gyrus_middle_occipital.name: Lateral occipital gyrus (Middle occipital gyrus*) (left)
lateral_occipital_gyrus_middle_occipital.description: The occipital gyri (OcG) are three gyri in parallel, along the lateral portion of the occipital lobe, also referred to as a composite structure in the brain. The gyri are the superior occipital gyrus, the middle occipital gyrus, and the inferior occipital gyrus, and these are also known as the occipital face area.

lateral_occipital_gyrus_middle_occipital.name: Lateral occipital gyrus (Middle occipital gyrus*) (right)
lateral_occipital_gyrus_middle_occipital.description: The occipital gyri (OcG) are three gyri in parallel, along the lateral portion of the occipital lobe, also referred to as a composite structure in the brain. The gyri are the superior occipital gyrus, the middle occipital gyrus, and the inferior occipital gyrus, and these are also known as the occipital face area.

lateral_occipitotemporal_gyrus_left.name: Lateral occipitotemporal gyrus (left)
lateral_occipitotemporal_gyrus_left.description: The fusiform gyrus, also known as the lateral occipitotemporal gyrus, is part of the temporal lobe and occipital lobe in Brodmann area 37. The fusiform gyrus is located between the lingual gyrus and parahippocampal gyrus above, and the inferior temporal gyrus below.

lateral_occipitotemporal_gyrus_right.name: Lateral occipitotemporal gyrus (right)
lateral_occipitotemporal_gyrus_right.description: The fusiform gyrus, also known as the lateral occipitotemporal gyrus, is part of the temporal lobe and occipital lobe in Brodmann area 37. The fusiform gyrus is located between the lingual gyrus and parahippocampal gyrus above, and the inferior temporal gyrus below.

lateral_pontine_branches_of_basilar_arte.name: Lateral pontine branches of basilar artery (left)
Lateral pontine branches of basilar artery (right)

lateral_process_of_nasal_septal_cartilag.name: Lateral process of nasal septal cartilage (left)
lateral_process_of_nasal_septal_cartilag.description: The lateral cartilage (upper lateral cartilage, lateral process of septal nasal cartilage) is situated below the inferior margin of the nasal bone, and is flattened, and triangular in shape.

lateral_process_of_nasal_septal_cartilag.name: Lateral process of nasal septal cartilage (right)
lateral_process_of_nasal_septal_cartilag.description: The lateral cartilage (upper lateral cartilage, lateral process of septal nasal cartilage) is situated below the inferior margin of the nasal bone, and is flattened, and triangular in shape.

lateral_rectus_muscle_left.name: Lateral rectus muscle (left)
lateral_rectus_muscle_left.description: The lateral rectus muscle is a muscle on the lateral side of the eye in the orbit. It is one of six extraocular muscles that control the movements of the eye. The lateral rectus muscle is responsible for lateral movement of the eyeball, specifically abduction. Abduction describes the movement of the eye away from the midline (i.a.

lateral_rectus_muscle_right.name: Lateral rectus muscle (right)
lateral_rectus_muscle_right.description: The lateral rectus muscle is a muscle on the lateral side of the eye in the orbit. It is one of six extraocular muscles that control the movements of the eye. The lateral rectus muscle is responsible for lateral movement of the eyeball, specifically abduction. Abduction describes the movement of the eye away from the midline (i.a.

lateral_region_of_neck_left.name: Lateral region of neck (left)
lateral_region_of_neck_left.description: By opposition to the anterior region of neck, the posterior region of neck, and the sternocleidomastoid region. The lateral region of neck includes: -the greater supraclavicular fossa -the omoclavicular triangle -the occipital triangle

lateral_region_of_neck_right.name: Lateral region of neck (right)
lateral_region_of_neck_right.description: By opposition to the anterior region of neck, the posterior region of neck, and the sternocleidomastoid region. The lateral region of neck includes: -the greater supraclavicular fossa -the omoclavicular triangle -the occipital triangle

lateral_temporomandibular_ligament_left.name: Lateral temporomandibular ligament (left)
lateral_temporomandibular_ligament_left.description: The temporomandibular ligament, also known as the external lateral ligament, is a ligament that connects the lower articular tubercle of the zygomatic arch to the lateral and posterior border of the neck of the mandible. It prevents posterior displacement of the mandible.

lateral_temporomandibular_ligament_right.name: Lateral temporomandibular ligament (right)
lateral_temporomandibular_ligament_right.description: The temporomandibular ligament, also known as the external lateral ligament, is a ligament that connects the lower articular tubercle of the zygomatic arch to the lateral and posterior border of the neck of the mandible. It prevents posterior displacement of the mandible.

lateral_thyrohyoid_ligament_left.name: Lateral thyrohyoid ligament (left)
lateral_thyrohyoid_ligament_left.description: The lateral thyrohyoid ligament (lateral hyothyroid ligament) is a round elastic cord, which forms the posterior border of the thyrohyoid membrane and passes between the tip of the superior cornu of the thyroid cartilage and the extremity of the greater cornu of the hyoid bone.

lateral_thyrohyoid_ligament_right.name: Lateral thyrohyoid ligament (right)
lateral_thyrohyoid_ligament_right.description: The lateral thyrohyoid ligament (lateral hyothyroid ligament) is a round elastic cord, which forms the posterior border of the thyrohyoid membrane and passes between the tip of the superior cornu of the thyroid cartilage and the extremity of the greater cornu of the hyoid bone.

lateral_ventricle_left.name: Lateral ventricle (left)
lateral_ventricle_left.description: The lateral ventricles are the two largest ventricles of the brain and contain cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Each cerebral hemisphere contains a lateral ventricle, known as the left or right ventricle, respectively.

lateral_ventricle_right.name: Lateral ventricle (right)
lateral_ventricle_right.description: The lateral ventricles are the two largest ventricles of the brain and contain cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Each cerebral hemisphere contains a lateral ventricle, known as the left or right ventricle, respectively.

lens_left.name: Lens (left)
lens_left.description: The lens is a transparent biconvex structure in the eye that, along with the cornea, helps to refract light to be focused on the retina.

lens_right.name: Lens (right)
lens_right.description: The lens is a transparent biconvex structure in the eye that, along with the cornea, helps to refract light to be focused on the retina.

levator_anguli_oris_left.name: Levator anguli oris (left)
levator_anguli_oris_left.description: The levator anguli oris (caninus) is a facial muscle of the mouth arising from the canine fossa, immediately below the infraorbital foramen. It elevates angle of mouth medially. Its fibers are inserted into the angle of the mouth, intermingling with those of the zygomaticus, triangularis, and orbicularis oris.

levator_anguli_oris_right.name: Levator anguli oris (right)
levator_anguli_oris_right.description: The levator anguli oris (caninus) is a facial muscle of the mouth arising from the canine fossa, immediately below the infraorbital foramen. It elevates angle of mouth medially. Its fibers are inserted into the angle of the mouth, intermingling with those of the zygomaticus, triangularis, and orbicularis oris.

levator_labii_superioris_left.name: Levator labii superioris (left)
levator_labii_superioris_left.description: The levator labii superioris (pl. levatores labii superioris, also called quadratus labii superioris, pl. quadrati labii superioris) is a muscle of the human body used in facial expression. It is a broad sheet, the origin of which extends from the side of the nose to the zygomatic bone.

levator_labii_superioris_right.name: Levator labii superioris (right)
levator_labii_superioris_right.description: The levator labii superioris (pl. levatores labii superioris, also called quadratus labii superioris, pl. quadrati labii superioris) is a muscle of the human body used in facial expression. It is a broad sheet, the origin of which extends from the side of the nose to the zygomatic bone.

levator_nasolabialis_left.name: Levator nasolabialis (left)
levator_nasolabialis_left.description: The levator labii superioris alaeque nasi muscle is, translated from Latin, the "lifter of both the upper lip and of the wing of the nose". It has the longest name of any muscle in an animal. The muscle is attached to the upper frontal process of the maxilla and inserts into the skin of the lateral part of the nostril and upper lip.

levator_nasolabialis_right.name: Levator nasolabialis (right)
levator_nasolabialis_right.description: The levator labii superioris alaeque nasi muscle is, translated from Latin, the "lifter of both the upper lip and of the wing of the nose". It has the longest name of any muscle in an animal. The muscle is attached to the upper frontal process of the maxilla and inserts into the skin of the lateral part of the nostril and upper lip.

levator_palpebrae_superioris_left.name: Levator palpebrae superioris (left)
levator_palpebrae_superioris_left.description: The levator palpebrae superioris (Latin: elevating muscle of upper eyelid) is the muscle in the orbit that elevates the upper eyelid.

levator_palpebrae_superioris_right.name: Levator palpebrae superioris (right)
levator_palpebrae_superioris_right.description: The levator palpebrae superioris (Latin: elevating muscle of upper eyelid) is the muscle in the orbit that elevates the upper eyelid.

lingual_nerve_left.name: Lingual nerve (left)
lingual_nerve_left.description: The lingual nerve carries sensory innervation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. It contains fibres from both the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3) and from the facial nerve (CN VII).

lingual_nerve_right.name: Lingual nerve (right)
lingual_nerve_right.description: The lingual nerve carries sensory innervation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. It contains fibres from both the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3) and from the facial nerve (CN VII).

lingula_of_cerebellum.name: Lingula of cerebellum
lingula_of_cerebellum.description: The lingula is a small tongue-shaped process, consisting of four or five folia; it lies in front of the lobulus centralis, and is concealed by it. Anteriorly, it rests on the dorsal surface of the anterior medullary velum, and its white substance is continuous with that of the velum. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingula_of_cerebellum

lobule_of_auricle_left.name: Lobule of auricle (left)
lobule_of_auricle_left.description: Inferior extremity of the auricle, without cartilage.

lobule_of_auricle_right.name: Lobule of auricle (right)
lobule_of_auricle_right.description: Inferior extremity of the auricle, without cartilage.

long_posterior_ciliary_arteries_left.name: Long posterior ciliary arteries (left)
long_posterior_ciliary_arteries_left.description: The long posterior ciliary arteries are arteries of the head arising, together with the other ciliary arteries, from the ophthalmic artery. There are two in each eye.

long_posterior_ciliary_arteries_right.name: Long posterior ciliary arteries (right)
long_posterior_ciliary_arteries_right.description: The long posterior ciliary arteries are arteries of the head arising, together with the other ciliary arteries, from the ophthalmic artery. There are two in each eye.

longissimus_capitis_muscle_left.name: Longissimus capitis muscle (left)
longissimus_capitis_muscle_left.description: The longissimus capitis (trachelomastoid muscle) lies medial to the longissimus cervicis, between it and the semispinalis capitis.

longissimus_capitis_muscle_right.name: Longissimus capitis muscle (right)
longissimus_capitis_muscle_right.description: The longissimus capitis (trachelomastoid muscle) lies medial to the longissimus cervicis, between it and the semispinalis capitis.

longus_capitis_muscle_left.name: Longus capitis muscle (left)
longus_capitis_muscle_left.description: The longus capitis muscle (Latin for long muscle of the head, alternatively rectus capitis anticus major), is broad and thick above, narrow below, and arises by four tendinous slips, from the anterior tubercles of the transverse processes of the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth cervical vertebræ, and ascends, converging toward its fellow of the opposite side, to be inserted into the inferior surface of the basilar part of the occipital bone.

longus_capitis_muscle_right.name: Longus capitis muscle (right)
longus_capitis_muscle_right.description: The longus capitis muscle (Latin for long muscle of the head, alternatively rectus capitis anticus major), is broad and thick above, narrow below, and arises by four tendinous slips, from the anterior tubercles of the transverse processes of the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth cervical vertebræ, and ascends, converging toward its fellow of the opposite side, to be inserted into the inferior surface of the basilar part of the occipital bone.

lower_canine_left.name: Lower canine (left)
lower_canine_left.description: In mammalian oral anatomy, the canine teeth, also called cuspids, dog teeth, or (in the context of the upper jaw) fangs, eye teeth, vampire teeth, or vampire fangs, are the relatively long, pointed teeth. They can appear more flattened however, causing them to resemble incisors and leading them to be called incisiform.

lower_canine_right.name: Lower canine (right)
lower_canine_right.description: In mammalian oral anatomy, the canine teeth, also called cuspids, dog teeth, or (in the context of the upper jaw) fangs, eye teeth, vampire teeth, or vampire fangs, are the relatively long, pointed teeth. They can appear more flattened however, causing them to resemble incisors and leading them to be called incisiform.

lower_first_molar_tooth_left.name: Lower first molar tooth (left)
lower_first_molar_tooth_left.description: The molars or molar teeth are large, flat teeth at the back of the mouth. They are more developed in mammals. They are used primarily to grind food during chewing. The name molar derives from Latin, molaris dens, meaning "millstone tooth", from mola, millstone and dens, tooth.

lower_first_molar_tooth_right.name: Lower first molar tooth (right)
lower_first_molar_tooth_right.description: The molars or molar teeth are large, flat teeth at the back of the mouth. They are more developed in mammals. lower_first_premolar_left.name: Lower first premolar (left)
lower_first_premolar_left.description: The premolars, also called premolar teeth, or bicuspids, are transitional teeth located between the canine and molar teeth. In humans, there are two premolars per quadrant in the permanent set of teeth, making eight premolars total in the mouth. They have at least two cusps.

lower_first_premolar_right.description: The premolars, also called premolar teeth, or bicuspids, are transitional teeth located between the canine and molar teeth. lower_lateral_incisor_left.name: Lower lateral incisor (left)
lower_lateral_incisor_left.description: Incisors (from Latin incidere, "to cut") are the front teeth present in most mammals. They are located in the premaxilla above and on the mandible below. Humans have a total of eight (two on each side, top and bottom). Opossums have 18, whereas armadillos have none.

lunate_sulcus_left.name: Lunate sulcus (left)
lunate_sulcus_left.description: In brain anatomy, the lunate sulcus or simian sulcus also known as the sulcus lunatus is a fissure in the occipital lobe variably found in humans and more often larger when present in apes and monkeys.

lunate_sulcus_right.name: Lunate sulcus (right)
lunate_sulcus_right.description: In brain anatomy, the lunate sulcus or simian sulcus also known as the sulcus lunatus is a fissure in the occipital lobe variably found in humans and more often larger when present in apes and monkeys.

major_alar_cartilage_left.name: Major alar cartilage (left)
major_alar_cartilage_left.description: The major alar cartilages are positioned with one structure on each side of the nasal tip. Superiorly, the major alar cartilages are connected to the lateral nasal cartilage via fibrous tissues. Composed of hyaline cartilage, these structures are very thin and folded to form the lateral and medial crus.

major_alar_cartilage_right.name: Major alar cartilage (right)
major_alar_cartilage_right.description: The major alar cartilages are positioned with one structure on each side of the nasal tip. Superiorly, the major alar cartilages are connected to the lateral nasal cartilage via fibrous tissues. Composed of hyaline cartilage, these structures are very thin and folded to form the lateral and medial crus.

mandible.name: Mandible
mandible.description: In anatomy, the mandible, lower jaw or jawbone is the largest, strongest and lowest bone in the human facial skeleton. It forms the lower jaw and holds the lower teeth in place. The mandible sits beneath the maxilla. It is the only movable bone of the skull (discounting the ossicles of the middle ear).

mandibular_node_left.name: Mandibular node (left)
mandibular_node_left.description: the mandibular node is located on the external side of the mandible.

mandibular_node_right.name: Mandibular node (right)
mandibular_node_right.description: the mandibular node is located on the external side of the mandible.

mastoid_nodes_left.name: Mastoid nodes (left)
mastoid_nodes_left.description: The mastoid lymph nodes (retroauricular lymph nodes or posterior auricular glands) are a small group of lymph nodes, usually two in number, located just beneath the ear, on the mastoid insertion of the sternocleidomastoideus muscle, beneath the posterior auricular muscle.

mastoid_nodes_right.name: Mastoid nodes (right)
mastoid_nodes_right.description: The mastoid lymph nodes (retroauricular lymph nodes or posterior auricular glands) are a small group of lymph nodes, usually two in number, located just beneath the ear, on the mastoid insertion of the sternocleidomastoideus muscle, beneath the posterior auricular muscle.

mastoid_region_left.name: Mastoid region (left)
mastoid_region_left.description: Behind the ear. See: Mastoid process

mastoid_region_right.name: Mastoid region (right)
mastoid_region_right.description: Behind the ear. See: Mastoid process

maxilla_left.name: Maxilla (left)
maxilla_left.description: The maxilla (plural: maxillae) in vertebrates is the upper fixed (not fixed in Neopterygii) bone of the jaw formed from the fusion of two maxillary bones. In humans, the upper jaw includes the hard palate in the front of the mouth. The two maxillary bones are fused at the intermaxillary suture, forming the anterior nasal spine.

maxilla_right.name: Maxilla (right)
maxilla_right.description: The maxilla (plural: maxillae) in vertebrates is the upper fixed (not fixed in Neopterygii) bone of the jaw formed from the fusion of two maxillary bones. In humans, the upper jaw includes the hard palate in the front of the mouth. The two maxillary bones are fused at the intermaxillary suture, forming the anterior nasal spine.

maxillary_artery_left.name: Maxillary artery (left)
maxillary_artery_left.description: The maxillary artery supplies deep structures of the face. It branches from the external carotid artery just deep to the neck of the mandible.

maxillary_artery_right.name: Maxillary artery (right)
maxillary_artery_right.description: The maxillary artery supplies deep structures of the face. It branches from the external carotid artery just deep to the neck of the mandible.

maxillary_nerve_left.name: Maxillary nerve (left)
maxillary_nerve_left.description: The maxillary nerve (V2) is one of the three branches or divisions of the trigeminal nerve, the fifth (CN V) cranial nerve.

maxillary_nerve_right.name: Maxillary nerve (right)
maxillary_nerve_right.description: The maxillary nerve (V2) is one of the three branches or divisions of the trigeminal nerve, the fifth (CN V) cranial nerve.

maxillary_veins_left.name: Maxillary veins (left)
maxillary_veins_left.description: The maxillary vein, or internal maxillary vein, is a vein of the head. It is a short trunk which accompanies the first part of the maxillary artery.

maxillary_veins_right.name: Maxillary veins (right)
maxillary_veins_right.description: The maxillary vein, or internal maxillary vein, is a vein of the head. It is a short trunk which accompanies the first part of the maxillary artery.

medial_geniculate_body_left.name: Medial geniculate body (left)
medial_geniculate_body_left.description: The medial geniculate nucleus (MGN) or medial geniculate body (MGB) is part of the auditory thalamus and represents the thalamic relay between the inferior colliculus (IC) and the auditory cortex (AC).

medial_geniculate_body_right.name: Medial geniculate body (right)
medial_geniculate_body_right.description: The medial geniculate nucleus (MGN) or medial geniculate body (MGB) is part of the auditory thalamus and represents the thalamic relay between the inferior colliculus (IC) and the auditory cortex (AC).

medial_occipital_artery_left.name: Medial occipital artery (left)
medial_occipital_artery_left.description: Medial terminal branch of the posterior cerebral artery. It goes to the medial surface of the occipital lobe. Feneis 248.18

medial_occipital_artery_right.name: Medial occipital artery (right)
medial_occipital_artery_right.description: Medial terminal branch of the posterior cerebral artery. It goes to the medial surface of the occipital lobe. Feneis 248.18

medial_occipitotemporal_gyrus_parahippoc.name: Medial occipitotemporal gyrus (Parahippocampal*) (left)
medial_occipitotemporal_gyrus_parahippoc.description: The parahippocampal gyrus (or hippocampal gyrus) is a grey matter cortical region of the brain that surrounds the hippocampus and is part of the limbic system. The region plays an important role in memory encoding and retrieval. It has been involved in some cases of hippocampal sclerosis. Asymmetry has been observed in schizophrenia.

medial_occipitotemporal_gyrus_parahippoc.name: Medial occipitotemporal gyrus (Parahippocampal*) (right)
medial_occipitotemporal_gyrus_parahippoc.description: The parahippocampal gyrus (or hippocampal gyrus) is a grey matter cortical region of the brain that surrounds the hippocampus and is part of the limbic system. The region plays an important role in memory encoding and retrieval. It has been involved in some cases of hippocampal sclerosis. Asymmetry has been observed in schizophrenia.

medial_pontine_branches_of_basilar_arter.name: Medial pontine branches of basilar artery (left)
Medial pontine branches of basilar artery (right)

medial_pterygoid_muscle_left.name: Medial pterygoid muscle (left)
medial_pterygoid_muscle_left.description: The medial pterygoid muscle (or internal pterygoid muscle), is a thick, quadrilateral muscle of the face. It is supplied by the mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve (V). It is important in mastication (chewing).

medial_pterygoid_muscle_right.name: Medial pterygoid muscle (right)
medial_pterygoid_muscle_right.description: The medial pterygoid muscle (or internal pterygoid muscle), is a thick, quadrilateral muscle of the face. It is supplied by the mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve (V). It is important in mastication (chewing).

medial_rectus_muscle_left.name: Medial rectus muscle (left)
medial_rectus_muscle_left.description: The medial rectus muscle is a muscle in the orbit near the eye. It is one of the extraocular muscles. It originates from the common tendinous ring, and inserts into the anteromedial surface of the eye. It is supplied by the inferior division of the oculomotor nerve (III). It rotates the eye medially (adduction).

medial_rectus_muscle_right.name: Medial rectus muscle (right)
medial_rectus_muscle_right.description: The medial rectus muscle is a muscle in the orbit near the eye. It is one of the extraocular muscles. It originates from the common tendinous ring, and inserts into the anteromedial surface of the eye. It is supplied by the inferior division of the oculomotor nerve (III). It rotates the eye medially (adduction).

median_thyrohyoid_ligament.name: Median thyrohyoid ligament
median_thyrohyoid_ligament.description: The median thyrohyoid ligament (also middle hyothyroid ligament or middle thyrohyoid ligament) is the thicker, middle part of the thyrohyoid membrane. Its lateral thinner portions are pierced by the superior laryngeal vessels and the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.

medulla_oblongata_left.name: Medulla oblongata (left)
medulla_oblongata_left.description: The medulla oblongata or simply medulla is a long stem-like structure which makes up the lower part of the brainstem. It is anterior and partially inferior to the cerebellum. It is a cone-shaped neuronal mass responsible for autonomic (involuntary) functions, ranging from vomiting to sneezing.

medulla_oblongata_right.name: Medulla oblongata (right)
medulla_oblongata_right.description: The medulla oblongata or simply medulla is a long stem-like structure which makes up the lower part of the brainstem. It is anterior and partially inferior to the cerebellum. It is a cone-shaped neuronal mass responsible for autonomic (involuntary) functions, ranging from vomiting to sneezing.

meningeal_branch_of_maxillary_nerve_left.name: Meningeal branch of maxillary nerve (left)
meningeal_branch_of_maxillary_nerve_left.description: MENINGEAL BRANCH OF THE MANDIBULAR NERVE (to be verified) The meningeal (recurrent) branch of the mandibular nerve (nervus spinosus) is a branch of the mandibular nerve that supplies the dura mater.

meningeal_branch_of_maxillary_nerve_righ.name: Meningeal branch of maxillary nerve (right)
meningeal_branch_of_maxillary_nerve_righ.description: MENINGEAL BRANCH OF THE MANDIBULAR NERVE (to be verified) The meningeal (recurrent) branch of the mandibular nerve (nervus spinosus) is a branch of the mandibular nerve that supplies the dura mater.

mental_branch_of_inferior_alveolar_arter.name: Mental branch of inferior alveolar artery (left)
Mental branch of inferior alveolar artery (right)

mental_nerve_left.name: Mental nerve (left)
mental_nerve_left.description: Mental nerve is a sensory nerve which provides sensation to the front of the chin and lower lip as well as the labial gingivae of the mandibular anterior teeth and the premolars. It is a branch of the posterior trunk of the inferior alveolar nerve, which is itself a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V).

mental_nerve_right.name: Mental nerve (right)
mental_nerve_right.description: Mental nerve is a sensory nerve which provides sensation to the front of the chin and lower lip as well as the labial gingivae of the mandibular anterior teeth and the premolars. It is a branch of the posterior trunk of the inferior alveolar nerve, which is itself a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V).

mental_region_left.name: Mental region (left)
mental_region_left.description: The chin is referred to as the mental region. See: Mental protuberance, Mandible, Gnathion

mental_region_right.name: Mental region (right)
mental_region_right.description: The chin is referred to as the mental region. See: Mental protuberance, Mandible, Gnathion

mentalis_muscle_left.name: Mentalis muscle (left)
mentalis_muscle_left.description: The mentalis muscle is a paired central muscle of the lower lip, situated at the tip of the chin. It originates from the mentum of the mandible, and inserts into the soft tissue of the chin. It is sometimes referred to as the "pouting muscle" due to it raising the lower lip and causing chin wrinkles.

mentalis_muscle_right.name: Mentalis muscle (right)
mentalis_muscle_right.description: The mentalis muscle is a paired central muscle of the lower lip, situated at the tip of the chin. It originates from the mentum of the mandible, and inserts into the soft tissue of the chin. It is sometimes referred to as the "pouting muscle" due to it raising the lower lip and causing chin wrinkles.

mentolabial_sulcus_left.name: Mentolabial sulcus (left)
mentolabial_sulcus_left.description: Depression between the lower lip and the chin.

mentolabial_sulcus_right.name: Mentolabial sulcus (right)
mentolabial_sulcus_right.description: Depression between the lower lip and the chin.

midbrain_left.name: Midbrain (left)
midbrain_left.description: The midbrain or mesencephalon is the forward-most portion of the brainstem and is associated with vision, hearing, motor control, sleep and wakefulness, arousal (alertness), and temperature regulation. The name comes from the Greek mesos, "middle", and enkephalos, "brain".

midbrain_right.name: Midbrain (right)
midbrain_right.description: The midbrain or mesencephalon is the forward-most portion of the brainstem and is associated with vision, hearing, motor control, sleep and wakefulness, arousal (alertness), and temperature regulation. middle_cerebral_artery_m1_segment_left.name: Middle cerebral artery (M1-segment) (left)
middle_cerebral_artery_m1_segment_left.description: The middle cerebral artery (MCA) is one of the three major paired arteries that supply blood to the cerebrum. The MCA arises from the internal carotid and continues into the lateral sulcus where it then branches and projects to many parts of the lateral cerebral cortex.

middle_cerebral_artery_m1_segment_right.name: Middle cerebral artery (M1-segment) (right)
middle_cerebral_artery_m1_segment_right.description: The middle cerebral artery (MCA) is one of the three major paired arteries that supply blood to the cerebrum. The MCA arises from the internal carotid and continues into the lateral sulcus where it then branches and projects to many parts of the lateral cerebral cortex.

middle_frontal_gyrus_left.name: Middle frontal gyrus (left)
middle_frontal_gyrus_left.description: The middle frontal gyrus makes up about one-third of the frontal lobe of the human brain. (A gyrus is one of the prominent "bumps" or "ridges" on the surface of the human brain.) The middle frontal gyrus, like the inferior frontal gyrus and the superior frontal gyrus, is more of a region in the frontal gyrus than a true gyrus.

middle_frontal_gyrus_right.name: Middle frontal gyrus (right)
middle_frontal_gyrus_right.description: The middle frontal gyrus makes up about one-third of the frontal lobe of the human brain. (A gyrus is one of the prominent "bumps" or "ridges" on the surface of the human brain.) The middle frontal gyrus, like the inferior frontal gyrus and the superior frontal gyrus, is more of a region in the frontal gyrus than a true gyrus.

middle_meningeal_artery_left.name: Middle meningeal artery (left)
middle_meningeal_artery_left.description: The middle meningeal artery (Latin: arteria meningea media) is typically the third branch of the first portion of the maxillary artery. After branching off the maxillary artery in the infratemporal fossa, it runs through the foramen spinosum to supply the dura mater (the outer meningeal layer) and the calvaria.

middle_meningeal_artery_right.name: Middle meningeal artery (right)
middle_meningeal_artery_right.description: The middle meningeal artery (Latin: arteria meningea media) is typically the third branch of the first portion of the maxillary artery. After branching off the maxillary artery in the infratemporal fossa, it runs through the foramen spinosum to supply the dura mater (the outer meningeal layer) and the calvaria.

middle_pharyngeal_constrictor_left.name: Middle pharyngeal constrictor (left)
middle_pharyngeal_constrictor_left.description: The middle pharyngeal constrictor is a fan-shaped muscle located in the neck. It is one of three pharyngeal constrictors. Similarly to the superior and inferior pharyngeal constrictor muscles, the middle pharyngeal constrictor is innervated by a branch of the vagus nerve through the pharyngeal plexus.

middle_pharyngeal_constrictor_right.name: Middle pharyngeal constrictor (right)
middle_pharyngeal_constrictor_right.description: The middle pharyngeal constrictor is a fan-shaped muscle located in the neck. It is one of three pharyngeal constrictors. Similarly to the superior and inferior pharyngeal constrictor muscles, the middle pharyngeal constrictor is innervated by a branch of the vagus nerve through the pharyngeal plexus.

middle_temporal_gyrus_left.name: Middle temporal gyrus (left)
middle_temporal_gyrus_left.description: Middle temporal gyrus is a gyrus in the brain on the temporal lobe. It is located between the superior temporal gyrus and inferior temporal gyrus. It corresponds largely to Brodmann area 21.

middle_temporal_gyrus_right.name: Middle temporal gyrus (right)
middle_temporal_gyrus_right.description: Middle temporal gyrus is a gyrus in the brain on the temporal lobe. It is located between the superior temporal gyrus and inferior temporal gyrus. It corresponds largely to Brodmann area 21.

motor_nucleus_of_facial_nerve_left.name: Motor nucleus of facial nerve (left)
motor_nucleus_of_facial_nerve_left.description: The facial motor nucleus is a collection of neurons in the brainstem that belong to the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII). These lower motor neurons innervate the muscles of facial expression and the stapedius.

motor_nucleus_of_facial_nerve_right.name: Motor nucleus of facial nerve (right)
motor_nucleus_of_facial_nerve_right.description: The facial motor nucleus is a collection of neurons in the brainstem that belong to the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII). These lower motor neurons innervate the muscles of facial expression and the stapedius.

motor_root_of_trigeminal_nerve_left.name: Motor root of trigeminal nerve (left)
motor_root_of_trigeminal_nerve_left.description: The trigeminal motor nucleus contains motor neurons that innervate muscles of the first branchial arch, namely the muscles of mastication, the tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini, mylohyoid, and anterior belly of the digastric. This nucleus is located in the mid-pons (i.e. in the center of the pons going inferior to superior).

motor_root_of_trigeminal_nerve_right.name: Motor root of trigeminal nerve (right)
motor_root_of_trigeminal_nerve_right.description: The trigeminal motor nucleus contains motor neurons that innervate muscles of the first branchial arch, namely the muscles of mastication, the tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini, mylohyoid, and anterior belly of the digastric. This nucleus is located in the mid-pons (i.e. in the center of the pons going inferior to superior).

multifidus_colli_muscle_left.name: Multifidus colli muscle (left)
multifidus_colli_muscle_left.description: The multifidus (multifidus spinae : pl. multifidi ) muscle consists of a number of fleshy and tendinous fasciculi, which fill up the groove on either side of the spinous processes of the vertebrae, from the sacrum to the axis. While very thin, the multifidus muscle plays an important role in stabilizing the joints within the spine.

multifidus_colli_muscle_right.name: Multifidus colli muscle (right)
multifidus_colli_muscle_right.description: The multifidus (multifidus spinae : pl. multifidi ) muscle consists of a number of fleshy and tendinous fasciculi, which fill up the groove on either side of the spinous processes of the vertebrae, from the sacrum to the axis. While very thin, the multifidus muscle plays an important role in stabilizing the joints within the spine.

mylohyoid_branch_of_inferior_alveolar_ar.name: Mylohyoid branch of inferior alveolar artery (left)
Mylohyoid branch of inferior alveolar artery (right)

mylohyoid_muscle_left.name: Mylohyoid muscle (left)
mylohyoid_muscle_left.description: The mylohyoid muscle or diaphragma oris is a paired muscle of the neck. It runs from the mandible to the hyoid bone, forming the floor of the oral cavity of the mouth. It is named after its two attachments near the molar teeth. It forms the floor of the submental triangle.

mylohyoid_muscle_right.name: Mylohyoid muscle (right)
mylohyoid_muscle_right.description: The mylohyoid muscle or diaphragma oris is a paired muscle of the neck. It runs from the mandible to the hyoid bone, forming the floor of the oral cavity of the mouth. It is named after its two attachments near the molar teeth. It forms the floor of the submental triangle.

nasal_bone_left.name: Nasal bone (left)
nasal_bone_left.description: The nasal bones are two small oblong bones, varying in size and form in different individuals; they are placed side by side at the middle and upper part of the face and by their junction, form the bridge of the upper one third of the nose. Each has two surfaces and four borders.

nasal_bone_right.name: Nasal bone (right)
nasal_bone_right.description: The nasal bones are two small oblong bones, varying in size and form in different individuals; they are placed side by side at the middle and upper part of the face and by their junction, form the bridge of the upper one third of the nose. Each has two surfaces and four borders.

nasal_region_left.name: Nasal region (left)
nasal_region_left.description: The nose is referred to as the nasal region.

nasal_region_right.name: Nasal region (right)
nasal_region_right.description: The nose is referred to as the nasal region.

nasal_septal_cartilage.name: Nasal septal cartilage
nasal_septal_cartilage.description: The nasal cartilages are structures within the nose that provide form and support to the nasal cavity. The nasal cartilages are made up of a flexible material called hyaline cartilage (packed collagen) in the distal portion of the nose.

nasalis_muscle_left.name: Nasalis muscle (left)
nasalis_muscle_left.description: The nasalis muscle is a sphincter-like muscle of the nose. It has a transverse part and an alar part. It compresses the nasal cartilages, and can "flare" the nostrils. Some people can use it to close the nostrils to prevent entry of water when underwater. It can be used to test the facial nerve (VII), which supplies it.

nasalis_muscle_right.name: Nasalis muscle (right)
nasalis_muscle_right.description: The nasalis muscle is a sphincter-like muscle of the nose. It has a transverse part and an alar part. It compresses the nasal cartilages, and can "flare" the nostrils. Some people can use it to close the nostrils to prevent entry of water when underwater. It can be used to test the facial nerve (VII), which supplies it.

nasolabial_node_left.name: Nasolabial node (left)
nasolabial_node_left.description: The nasolabial lymph node is a facial node found near the nose and upper lip. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasolabial_lymph_node

nasolabial_node_right.name: Nasolabial node (right)
nasolabial_node_right.description: The nasolabial lymph node is a facial node found near the nose and upper lip. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasolabial_lymph_node

nasolabial_sulcus_left.name: Nasolabial sulcus (left)
nasolabial_sulcus_left.description: Groove from the ala of nose to the angle of mouth. See: Oral region

nasolabial_sulcus_right.name: Nasolabial sulcus (right)
nasolabial_sulcus_right.description: Groove from the ala of nose to the angle of mouth. See: Oral region

nasolacrimal_duct_left.name: Nasolacrimal duct (left)
nasolacrimal_duct_left.description: The nasolacrimal duct (also called the tear duct) carries tears from the lacrimal sac of the eye into the nasal cavity. The duct begins in the eye socket between the maxillary and lacrimal bones, from where it passes downwards and backwards.

nasolacrimal_duct_right.name: Nasolacrimal duct (right)
nasolacrimal_duct_right.description: The nasolacrimal duct (also called the tear duct) carries tears from the lacrimal sac of the eye into the nasal cavity. The duct begins in the eye socket between the maxillary and lacrimal bones, from where it passes downwards and backwards.

nasopharynx.name: Nasopharynx
nasopharynx.description: The upper portion of the pharynx, the nasopharynx, extends from the base of the skull to the upper surface of the soft palate. It includes the space between the internal nares and the soft palate and lies above the oral cavity.

neurohypophysis.name: Neurohypophysis
neurohypophysis.description: The posterior pituitary (or neurohypophysis) is the posterior lobe of the pituitary gland which is part of the endocrine system. The posterior pituitary is not glandular as is the anterior pituitary.

nodule_of_vermis.name: Nodule of vermis
nodule_of_vermis.description: The nodule (nodular lobe), or anterior end of the inferior vermis, abuts against the roof of the fourth ventricle, and can only be distinctly seen after the cerebellum has been separated from the medulla oblongata and pons. On either side of the nodule is a thin layer of white substance, named the posterior medullary velum.

nuchal_ligament.name: Nuchal ligament
nuchal_ligament.description: The nuchal ligament is a ligament at the back of the neck that is continuous with the supraspinous ligament.

nucleus_ambiguus_left.name: Nucleus ambiguus (left)
nucleus_ambiguus_left.description: The nucleus ambiguus ("ambiguous nucleus" in English) is a group of large motor neurons, situated deep in the medullary reticular formation named by Jacob Clarke. The nucleus ambiguus contains the cell bodies of neurons that innervate the muscles of the soft palate, pharynx, and larynx which are associated with speech and swallowing.

nucleus_ambiguus_right.name: Nucleus ambiguus (right)
nucleus_ambiguus_right.description: The nucleus ambiguus ("ambiguous nucleus" in English) is a group of large motor neurons, situated deep in the medullary reticular formation named by Jacob Clarke. The nucleus ambiguus contains the cell bodies of neurons that innervate the muscles of the soft palate, pharynx, and larynx which are associated with speech and swallowing.

nucleus_of_abducens_nerve_left.name: Nucleus of abducens nerve (left)
nucleus_of_abducens_nerve_left.description: The abducens nucleus is the originating nucleus from which the abducens nerve (VI) emerges—a cranial nerve nucleus. This nucleus is located beneath the fourth ventricle in the caudal portion of the pons, medial to the sulcus limitans.

nucleus_of_abducens_nerve_right.name: Nucleus of abducens nerve (right)
nucleus_of_abducens_nerve_right.description: The abducens nucleus is the originating nucleus from which the abducens nerve (VI) emerges—a cranial nerve nucleus. This nucleus is located beneath the fourth ventricle in the caudal portion of the pons, medial to the sulcus limitans.

nucleus_of_accessory_nerve_left.name: Nucleus of accessory nerve (left)
nucleus_of_accessory_nerve_left.description: The spinal accessory nucleus lies within the cervical spinal cord (C1-C5) in the posterolateral aspect of the anterior horn. The nucleus ambiguus is classically said to provide the "cranial component" of the accessory nerve.

nucleus_of_accessory_nerve_right.name: Nucleus of accessory nerve (right)
nucleus_of_accessory_nerve_right.description: The spinal accessory nucleus lies within the cervical spinal cord (C1-C5) in the posterolateral aspect of the anterior horn. The nucleus ambiguus is classically said to provide the "cranial component" of the accessory nerve.

nucleus_of_hypoglossal_nerve_left.name: Nucleus of hypoglossal nerve (left)
nucleus_of_hypoglossal_nerve_left.description: The hypoglossal nucleus is a cranial nerve nucleus, found within the medulla. Being a motor nucleus, it is close to the midline. In the open medulla, it is visible as what is known as the hypoglossal trigone, a raised area (medial to the vagal trigone) protruding slightly into the fourth ventricle.

nucleus_of_hypoglossal_nerve_right.name: Nucleus of hypoglossal nerve (right)
nucleus_of_hypoglossal_nerve_right.description: The hypoglossal nucleus is a cranial nerve nucleus, found within the medulla. Being a motor nucleus, it is close to the midline. In the open medulla, it is visible as what is known as the hypoglossal trigone, a raised area (medial to the vagal trigone) protruding slightly into the fourth ventricle.

nucleus_of_oculomotor_nerve_left.name: Nucleus of oculomotor nerve (left)
nucleus_of_oculomotor_nerve_left.description: The fibers of the oculomotor nerve arise from a nucleus in the midbrain, which lies in the gray substance of the floor of the cerebral aqueduct and extends in front of the aqueduct for a short distance into the floor of the third ventricle.

nucleus_of_oculomotor_nerve_right.name: Nucleus of oculomotor nerve (right)
nucleus_of_oculomotor_nerve_right.description: The fibers of the oculomotor nerve arise from a nucleus in the midbrain, which lies in the gray substance of the floor of the cerebral aqueduct and extends in front of the aqueduct for a short distance into the floor of the third ventricle.

nucleus_of_trochlear_nerve_left.name: Nucleus of trochlear nerve (left)
nucleus_of_trochlear_nerve_left.description: The nucleus of the trochlear nerve () is located in the midbrain, at an intercollicular level between the superior colliculus and inferior colliculus. It is a motor nucleus, and so is located near the midline, embedded within the medial longitudinal fasciculus (see diagram at right).

nucleus_of_trochlear_nerve_right.name: Nucleus of trochlear nerve (right)
nucleus_of_trochlear_nerve_right.description: The nucleus of the trochlear nerve () is located in the midbrain, at an intercollicular level between the superior colliculus and inferior colliculus. It is a motor nucleus, and so is located near the midline, embedded within the medial longitudinal fasciculus (see diagram at right).

obliquus_inferior_capitis_muscle_left.name: Obliquus inferior capitis muscle (left)
obliquus_inferior_capitis_muscle_left.description: The obliquus capitis inferior muscle (/əˈblaɪkwəs ˈkæpɪtɪs/) is the larger of the two oblique muscles of the neck. It arises from the apex of the spinous process of the axis and passes laterally and slightly upward, to be inserted into the lower and back part of the transverse process of the atlas.

obliquus_inferior_capitis_muscle_right.name: Obliquus inferior capitis muscle (right)
obliquus_inferior_capitis_muscle_right.description: The obliquus capitis inferior muscle (/əˈblaɪkwəs ˈkæpɪtɪs/) is the larger of the two oblique muscles of the neck. It arises from the apex of the spinous process of the axis and passes laterally and slightly upward, to be inserted into the lower and back part of the transverse process of the atlas.

obliquus_superior_capitis_muscle_left.name: Obliquus superior capitis muscle (left)
obliquus_superior_capitis_muscle_left.description: The obliquus capitis superior muscle (/əˈblaɪkwəs ˈkæpɪtɪs/) is a small muscle in the upper back part of the neck and is one of the suboccipital muscles and part of the suboccipital triangle. It arises from the lateral mass of the atlas bone.

obliquus_superior_capitis_muscle_right.name: Obliquus superior capitis muscle (right)
obliquus_superior_capitis_muscle_right.description: The obliquus capitis superior muscle (/əˈblaɪkwəs ˈkæpɪtɪs/) is a small muscle in the upper back part of the neck and is one of the suboccipital muscles and part of the suboccipital triangle. It arises from the lateral mass of the atlas bone.

occipital_artery_left.name: Occipital artery (left)
occipital_artery_left.description: The occipital artery arises from the external carotid artery opposite the facial artery. Its path is below the posterior belly of digastric to the occipital region. This artery supplies blood to the back of the scalp and sternocleidomastoid muscles, and deep muscles in the back and neck.

occipital_artery_right.name: Occipital artery (right)
occipital_artery_right.description: The occipital artery arises from the external carotid artery opposite the facial artery. Its path is below the posterior belly of digastric to the occipital region. This artery supplies blood to the back of the scalp and sternocleidomastoid muscles, and deep muscles in the back and neck.

occipital_bone.name: Occipital bone
occipital_bone.description: The occipital bone () is a cranial dermal bone and the main bone of the occiput (back and lower part of the skull). It is trapezoidal in shape and curved on itself like a shallow dish. The occipital bone overlies the occipital lobes of the cerebrum.

occipital_nodes_left.name: Occipital nodes (left)
occipital_nodes_left.description: The occipital lymph nodes, one to three in number, are located on the back of the head close to the margin of the trapezius and resting on the insertion of the semispinalis capitis. Their afferent vessels drain the occipital region of the scalp, while their efferents pass to the superior deep cervical glands.

occipital_nodes_right.name: Occipital nodes (right)
occipital_nodes_right.description: The occipital lymph nodes, one to three in number, are located on the back of the head close to the margin of the trapezius and resting on the insertion of the semispinalis capitis. Their afferent vessels drain the occipital region of the scalp, while their efferents pass to the superior deep cervical glands.

occipital_pole_left.name: Occipital pole (left)
occipital_pole_left.description: There are three known poles of the cerebral hemispheres: the occipital pole, the frontal pole, and the temporal pole.

occipital_pole_right.name: Occipital pole (right)
occipital_pole_right.description: There are three known poles of the cerebral hemispheres: the occipital pole, the frontal pole, and the temporal pole.

occipital_region_left.name: Occipital region (left)
occipital_region_left.description: Back of the head. See: Occipital bone, occiput

occipital_region_right.name: Occipital region (right)
occipital_region_right.description: Back of the head. See: Occipital bone, occiput

occipital_vein_left.name: Occipital vein (left)
occipital_vein_left.description: The occipital vein is a vein of the scalp. It originates from a plexus around the external occipital protuberance and superior nuchal line to the back part of the vertex of the skull. It usually drains into the internal jugular vein, but may also drain into the posterior auricular vein (which joins the external jugular vein).

occipital_vein_right.name: Occipital vein (right)
occipital_vein_right.description: The occipital vein is a vein of the scalp. It originates from a plexus around the external occipital protuberance and superior nuchal line to the back part of the vertex of the skull. It usually drains into the internal jugular vein, but may also drain into the posterior auricular vein (which joins the external jugular vein).

occipitalis_muscle_left.name: Occipitalis muscle (left)
occipitalis_muscle_left.description: The occipitalis muscle (occipital belly) is a muscle which covers parts of the skull. Some sources consider the occipital muscle to be a distinct muscle. However, Terminologia Anatomica currently classifies it as part of the occipitofrontalis muscle along with the frontalis muscle. The occipitalis muscle is thin and quadrilateral in form.

occipitalis_muscle_right.name: Occipitalis muscle (right)
occipitalis_muscle_right.description: The occipitalis muscle (occipital belly) is a muscle which covers parts of the skull. Some sources consider the occipital muscle to be a distinct muscle. However, Terminologia Anatomica currently classifies it as part of the occipitofrontalis muscle along with the frontalis muscle. The occipitalis muscle is thin and quadrilateral in form.

oculomotor_nerve_iii_left.name: Oculomotor nerve (III) (left)
oculomotor_nerve_iii_left.description: The oculomotor nerve is the third cranial nerve (CN III). It enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure and innervates extrinsic eye muscles that enable most movements of the eye and that raise the eyelid.

oculomotor_nerve_iii_right.name: Oculomotor nerve (III) (right)
oculomotor_nerve_iii_right.description: The oculomotor nerve is the third cranial nerve (CN III). It enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure and innervates extrinsic eye muscles that enable most movements of the eye and that raise the eyelid.

olfactory_nerve_i_left.name: Olfactory nerve (I) (left)
olfactory_nerve_i_left.description: The olfactory nerve is typically considered the first cranial nerve, or simply CN I, that contains sensory nerve fibers relating to the sense of smell. The afferent nerve fibers of the olfactory receptor neurons transmit nerve impulses about odors to the central nervous system (olfaction).

olfactory_nerve_i_right.name: Olfactory nerve (I) (right)
olfactory_nerve_i_right.description: The olfactory nerve is typically considered the first cranial nerve, or simply CN I, that contains sensory nerve fibers relating to the sense of smell. The afferent nerve fibers of the olfactory receptor neurons transmit nerve impulses about odors to the central nervous system (olfaction).

olfactory_sulcus_left.name: Olfactory sulcus (left)
olfactory_sulcus_left.description: The olfactory tract is a bilateral bundle of afferent nerve fibers from the mitral and tufted cells of the olfactory bulb that connects to several target regions in the brain, including the piriform cortex, amygdala, and entorhinal cortex. It is a narrow white band, triangular on coronal section, the apex being directed upward.

olfactory_sulcus_right.name: Olfactory sulcus (right)
olfactory_sulcus_right.description: The olfactory tract is a bilateral bundle of afferent nerve fibers from the mitral and tufted cells of the olfactory bulb that connects to several target regions in the brain, including the piriform cortex, amygdala, and entorhinal cortex. It is a narrow white band, triangular on coronal section, the apex being directed upward.

olive_left.name: Olive (left)
olive_left.description: In anatomy, the olivary bodies or simply olives (Latin oliva and olivae, singular and plural, respectively) are a pair of prominent oval structures in the medulla oblongata, the lower portion of the brainstem. They contain the olivary nuclei.

olive_right.name: Olive (right)
olive_right.description: In anatomy, the olivary bodies or simply olives (Latin oliva and olivae, singular and plural, respectively) are a pair of prominent oval structures in the medulla oblongata, the lower portion of the brainstem. They contain the olivary nuclei.

opercular_part_of_inferior_frontal_gyrus.name: Opercular part of inferior frontal gyrus (left)
opercular_part_of_inferior_frontal_gyrus.description: The inferior frontal gyrus is highly convoluted and has three cytoarchitecturally diverse regions. The three subdivisions are an opercular part, a triangular part, and an orbital part. These divisions are marked by two rami arising from the lateral sulcus. The ascending ramus separates the opercular and triangular parts.

opercular_part_of_inferior_frontal_gyrus.name: Opercular part of inferior frontal gyrus (right)
opercular_part_of_inferior_frontal_gyrus.description: The inferior frontal gyrus is highly convoluted and has three cytoarchitecturally diverse regions. The three subdivisions are an opercular part, a triangular part, and an orbital part. These divisions are marked by two rami arising from the lateral sulcus. The ascending ramus separates the opercular and triangular parts.

ophthalmic_artery_left.name: Ophthalmic artery (left)
ophthalmic_artery_left.description: The ophthalmic artery (OA) is an artery of the head. It is the first branch of the internal carotid artery distal to the cavernous sinus. Branches of the ophthalmic artery supply all the structures in the orbit around the eye, as well as some structures in the nose, face, and meninges.

ophthalmic_artery_right.name: Ophthalmic artery (right)
ophthalmic_artery_right.description: The ophthalmic artery (OA) is an artery of the head. It is the first branch of the internal carotid artery distal to the cavernous sinus. Branches of the ophthalmic artery supply all the structures in the orbit around the eye, as well as some structures in the nose, face, and meninges.

ophthalmic_nerve_left.name: Ophthalmic nerve (left)
ophthalmic_nerve_left.description: The ophthalmic nerve (V1) is a sensory nerve of the face. It is one of three divisions of the trigeminal nerve (CN V). It has three branches that provide sensory innervation to the eye, the skin of the upper face, and the skin of the anterior scalp.

ophthalmic_nerve_right.name: Ophthalmic nerve (right)
ophthalmic_nerve_right.description: The ophthalmic nerve (V1) is a sensory nerve of the face. It is one of three divisions of the trigeminal nerve (CN V). It has three branches that provide sensory innervation to the eye, the skin of the upper face, and the skin of the anterior scalp.

optic_chiasm_left.name: Optic chiasm (left)
optic_chiasm_left.description: The optic chiasm, or optic chiasma is the part of the brain where the optic nerves cross. It is located at the bottom of the brain immediately inferior to the hypothalamus. The optic chiasm is found in all vertebrates, although in cyclostomes (lampreys and hagfishes), it is located within the brain.

optic_chiasm_right.name: Optic chiasm (right)
optic_chiasm_right.description: The optic chiasm, or optic chiasma is the part of the brain where the optic nerves cross. It is located at the bottom of the brain immediately inferior to the hypothalamus. The optic chiasm is found in all vertebrates, although in cyclostomes (lampreys and hagfishes), it is located within the brain.

optic_nerve_ii_left.name: Optic nerve (II) (left)
optic_nerve_ii_left.description: The optic nerve, also known as cranial nerve II, or simply as CN II, is a paired cranial nerve that transmits visual information from the retina to the brain.

optic_nerve_ii_right.name: Optic nerve (II) (right)
optic_nerve_ii_right.description: The optic nerve, also known as cranial nerve II, or simply as CN II, is a paired cranial nerve that transmits visual information from the retina to the brain.

optic_tract_left.name: Optic tract (left)
optic_tract_left.description: The optic tract (from the Latin tractus opticus) is a part of the visual system in the brain. It is a continuation of the optic nerve that relays information from the optic chiasm to the ipsilateral lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN), pretectal nuclei, and superior colliculus.

optic_tract_right.name: Optic tract (right)
optic_tract_right.description: The optic tract (from the Latin tractus opticus) is a part of the visual system in the brain. It is a continuation of the optic nerve that relays information from the optic chiasm to the ipsilateral lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN), pretectal nuclei, and superior colliculus.

oral_region_left.name: Oral region (left)
oral_region_left.description: The mouth is referred to as the oral region; it is one of the regions of the face. Several structures are parts of the oral region: -Philtrum -Tubercle of upper lip -Labial commissure -Angle of mouth

oral_region_right.name: Oral region (right)
oral_region_right.description: The mouth is referred to as the oral region; it is one of the regions of the face. Several structures are parts of the oral region: -Philtrum -Tubercle of upper lip -Labial commissure -Angle of mouth

orbicularis_oris_muscle_left.name: Orbicularis oris muscle (left)
orbicularis_oris_muscle_left.description: In human anatomy, the orbicularis oris muscle is a complex of muscles in the lips that encircles the mouth. It is a sphincter, or circular muscle, but it is actually composed of four independent quadrants that interlace and give only an appearance of circularity.

orbicularis_oris_muscle_right.name: Orbicularis oris muscle (right)

orbital_gyri_frontomarginal_gyrus_and_su.description: The inferior or orbital surface of the frontal lobe is concave, and rests on the orbital plate of the frontal bone. It is divided into four orbital gyri by a well-marked H-shaped orbital sulcus. These are named, from their position, the medial, anterior, lateral, and posterior, orbital gyri.

orbital_gyri_frontomarginal_gyrus_and_su.name: Orbital gyri (Frontomarginal gyrus and sulcus*) (right)

orbital_part_of_inferior_frontal_gyrus_l.name: Orbital part of  inferior frontal gyrus (left)
orbital_part_of_inferior_frontal_gyrus_l.description: Orbital part of inferior frontal gyrus (pars orbitalis) (cortex inferior and anterior to the horizontal ramus of the lateral sulcus). The orbital part of the inferior frontal gyrus is known as Brodmann area 47.

orbital_part_of_inferior_frontal_gyrus_r.name: Orbital part of  inferior frontal gyrus (right)
orbital_part_of_inferior_frontal_gyrus_r.description: Orbital part of inferior frontal gyrus (pars orbitalis) (cortex inferior and anterior to the horizontal ramus of the lateral sulcus). The orbital part of the inferior frontal gyrus is known as Brodmann area 47.

orbital_part_of_orbicularis_oculi_left.name: Orbital part of orbicularis oculi (left)
orbital_part_of_orbicularis_oculi_left.description: The orbicularis oculi is a muscle in the face that closes the eyelids. It arises from the nasal part of the frontal bone, from the frontal process of the maxilla in front of the lacrimal groove, and from the anterior surface and borders of a short fibrous band, the medial palpebral ligament.

Orbitofrontal branches of anterior cerebral artery (right)

oropharynx.name: Oropharynx
oropharynx.description: The oropharynx lies behind the oral cavity, extending from the uvula to the level of the hyoid bone. It opens anteriorly, through the isthmus faucium, into the mouth, while in its lateral wall, between the palatoglossal arch and the palatopharyngeal arch, is the palatine tonsil.

palatine_bone_left.name: Palatine bone (left)
palatine_bone_left.description: In anatomy, the palatine bones () are two irregular bones of the facial skeleton in many animal species, located above the uvula in the throat. Together with the maxillae, they comprise the hard palate. (Palate is derived from the Latin palatum.)

palatine_bone_right.name: Palatine bone (right)
palatine_bone_right.description: In anatomy, the palatine bones () are two irregular bones of the facial skeleton in many animal species, located above the uvula in the throat. Together with the maxillae, they comprise the hard palate. (Palate is derived from the Latin palatum.)

palatine_tonsil_left.name: Palatine tonsil (left)
palatine_tonsil_left.description: Palatine tonsils, commonly called the tonsils and occasionally called the faucial tonsils, are tonsils located on the left and right sides at the back of the throat, which can often be seen as flesh-colored, pinkish lumps.

palatine_tonsil_right.name: Palatine tonsil (right)
palatine_tonsil_right.description: Palatine tonsils, commonly called the tonsils and occasionally called the faucial tonsils, are tonsils located on the left and right sides at the back of the throat, which can often be seen as flesh-colored, pinkish lumps.

palatopharyngeus_muscle_left.name: Palatopharyngeus muscle (left)
palatopharyngeus_muscle_left.description: The palatopharyngeus (palatopharyngeal or pharyngopalatinus) muscle is a small muscle in the roof of the mouth. It is a long, fleshy fasciculus, narrower in the middle than at either end, forming, with the mucous membrane covering its surface, the palatopharyngeal arch.

palatopharyngeus_muscle_right.name: Palatopharyngeus muscle (right)
palatopharyngeus_muscle_right.description: The palatopharyngeus (palatopharyngeal or pharyngopalatinus) muscle is a small muscle in the roof of the mouth. It is a long, fleshy fasciculus, narrower in the middle than at either end, forming, with the mucous membrane covering its surface, the palatopharyngeal arch.

paracentral_gyrus_and_sulcus_left.description: The paracentral sulcus is a sulcus of the brain. It forms the paracentral lobule's anterior border. It is part of the cingulate sulcus. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paracentral_sulcus

paracentral_gyrus_and_sulcus_right.name: Paracentral gyrus and sulcus* (right)
paracentral_gyrus_and_sulcus_right.description: The paracentral sulcus is a sulcus of the brain. It forms the paracentral lobule's anterior border. It is part of the cingulate sulcus. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paracentral_sulcus

parietal_bone_left.description: The parietal bones are two bones in the skull which, when joined together at a fibrous joint, form the sides and roof of the cranium.
