Parietal branches of middle cerebral artery (right)

parietal_region_left.name: Parietal region (left)
parietal_region_left.description: Postero-superior part of the head, between the frontal region, the occipital region, and the two temporal regions.

parietal_region_right.name: Parietal region (right)
parietal_region_right.description: Postero-superior part of the head, between the frontal region, the occipital region, and the two temporal regions.

parieto_occipital_artery_left.name: Parieto-occipital artery (left)
parieto_occipital_artery_left.description: Branch running in the parieto-occipital sulcus distributing itself to the superior part of the cuneus and a posterior part of the precuneus. Feneis 248.21

parieto_occipital_artery_right.name: Parieto-occipital artery (right)
parieto_occipital_artery_right.description: Branch running in the parieto-occipital sulcus distributing itself to the superior part of the cuneus and a posterior part of the precuneus. Feneis 248.21

parieto_occipital_sulcus_left.name: Parieto-occipital sulcus (left)
parieto_occipital_sulcus_left.description: The parieto-occipital sulcus (also called the parieto-occipital fissure) is a deep sulcus in the cerebral cortex that marks the boundary between the cuneus and precuneus, and also between the parietal and occipital lobes. Only a small part can be seen on the lateral surface of the hemisphere, its chief part being on the medial surface.

parieto_occipital_sulcus_right.name: Parieto-occipital sulcus (right)
parieto_occipital_sulcus_right.description: The parieto-occipital sulcus (also called the parieto-occipital fissure) is a deep sulcus in the cerebral cortex that marks the boundary between the cuneus and precuneus, and also between the parietal and occipital lobes. Only a small part can be seen on the lateral surface of the hemisphere, its chief part being on the medial surface.

parotid_duct_left.name: Parotid duct (left)
parotid_duct_left.description: The parotid duct, or Stensen duct,is a salivary duct. It is the route that saliva takes from the major salivary gland, the parotid gland, into the mouth.

parotid_duct_right.name: Parotid duct (right)
parotid_duct_right.description: The parotid duct, or Stensen duct,is a salivary duct. It is the route that saliva takes from the major salivary gland, the parotid gland, into the mouth.

parotid_gland_left.name: Parotid gland (left)
parotid_gland_left.description: The parotid gland is a major salivary gland in many animals. In humans, the two parotid glands are present on either side of the mouth and in front of both ears. They are the largest of the salivary glands.

parotid_gland_right.name: Parotid gland (right)
parotid_gland_right.description: The parotid gland is a major salivary gland in many animals. In humans, the two parotid glands are present on either side of the mouth and in front of both ears. They are the largest of the salivary glands.

pericallosal_artery_left.name: Pericallosal artery (left)
pericallosal_artery_left.description: A3, also termed the pericallosal artery, is one of the (or the only) main terminal branches of the ACA, which extends posteriorly in the pericallosal sulcus to form the internal parietal arteries (superior, inferior) and the precuneal artery. This artery may form an anastomosis with the posterior cerebral artery.

pericallosal_artery_right.name: Pericallosal artery (right)
pericallosal_artery_right.description: A3, also termed the pericallosal artery, is one of the (or the only) main terminal branches of the ACA, which extends posteriorly in the pericallosal sulcus to form the internal parietal arteries (superior, inferior) and the precuneal artery. This artery may form an anastomosis with the posterior cerebral artery.

philtrum_left.name: Philtrum (left)
philtrum_left.description: The philtrum (Latin: philtrum from Ancient Greek φίλτρον phíltron, lit. "love charm"), or medial cleft, is a vertical indentation in the middle area of the upper lip, common to therian mammals, extending in humans from the nasal septum to the tubercle of the upper lip.

philtrum_right.name: Philtrum (right)
philtrum_right.description: The philtrum (Latin: philtrum from Ancient Greek φίλτρον phíltron, lit. "love charm"), or medial cleft, is a vertical indentation in the middle area of the upper lip, common to therian mammals, extending in humans from the nasal septum to the tubercle of the upper lip.

pineal_gland.name: Pineal gland
pineal_gland.description: The pineal gland, conarium, or epiphysis cerebri, is a small endocrine gland in the brain of most vertebrates. The pineal gland produces melatonin, a serotonin-derived hormone which modulates sleep patterns in both circadian and seasonal cycles. The shape of the gland resembles a pine cone, which gives it its name.

pons_left.name: Pons (left)
pons_left.description: The pons (from Latin pons, "bridge") is part of the brainstem that in humans and other bipeds lies inferior to the midbrain, superior to the medulla oblongata and anterior to the cerebellum. The pons is also called the pons Varolii ("bridge of Varolius"), after the Italian anatomist and surgeon Costanzo Varolio (1543–75).

pons_right.name: Pons (right)
pons_right.description: The pons (from Latin pons, "bridge") is part of the brainstem that in humans and other bipeds lies inferior to the midbrain, superior to the medulla oblongata and anterior to the cerebellum. The pons is also called the pons Varolii ("bridge of Varolius"), after the Italian anatomist and surgeon Costanzo Varolio (1543–75).

postcentral_gyrus_left.name: Postcentral gyrus (left)
postcentral_gyrus_left.description: The postcentral gyrus is a prominent gyrus in the lateral parietal lobe of the human brain. It is the location of the primary somatosensory cortex, the main sensory receptive area for the sense of touch. Like other sensory areas, there is a map of sensory space in this location, called the sensory homunculus.

postcentral_gyrus_right.name: Postcentral gyrus (right)
postcentral_gyrus_right.description: The postcentral gyrus is a prominent gyrus in the lateral parietal lobe of the human brain. It is the location of the primary somatosensory cortex, the main sensory receptive area for the sense of touch. Like other sensory areas, there is a map of sensory space in this location, called the sensory homunculus.

postcentral_sulcus_left.name: Postcentral sulcus (left)
postcentral_sulcus_left.description: The postcentral sulcus of the parietal lobe lies parallel to, and behind, the central sulcus in the human brain. (A sulcus is one of the prominent grooves on the surface of the brain.) The postcentral sulcus divides the postcentral gyrus from the remainder of the parietal lobe. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postcentral_sulcus

postcentral_sulcus_right.name: Postcentral sulcus (right)
postcentral_sulcus_right.description: The postcentral sulcus of the parietal lobe lies parallel to, and behind, the central sulcus in the human brain. (A sulcus is one of the prominent grooves on the surface of the brain.) The postcentral sulcus divides the postcentral gyrus from the remainder of the parietal lobe. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postcentral_sulcus

posterior_auricular_groove_left.name: Posterior auricular groove (left)
posterior_auricular_groove_left.description: Shallow depression between the antitragus and the antihelix.

posterior_auricular_groove_right.name: Posterior auricular groove (right)
posterior_auricular_groove_right.description: Shallow depression between the antitragus and the antihelix.

posterior_auricular_vein_left.name: Posterior auricular vein (left)
posterior_auricular_vein_left.description: The posterior auricular vein is a vein of the head. It begins from a plexus with the occipital vein and the superficial temporal vein, descends behind the auricle, and drains into the external jugular vein.

posterior_auricular_vein_right.name: Posterior auricular vein (right)
posterior_auricular_vein_right.description: The posterior auricular vein is a vein of the head. It begins from a plexus with the occipital vein and the superficial temporal vein, descends behind the auricle, and drains into the external jugular vein.

posterior_belly_of_digastric_muscle_left.name: Posterior belly of digastric muscle (left)
posterior_belly_of_digastric_muscle_left.description: The digastric muscle (also digastricus) (named digastric as it has two 'bellies') is a small muscle located under the jaw. The term "digastric muscle" refers to this specific muscle. However, other muscles that have two separate muscle bellies include the suspensory muscle of duodenum, omohyoid, occipitofrontalis.

posterior_belly_of_digastric_muscle_righ.name: Posterior belly of digastric muscle (right)
posterior_belly_of_digastric_muscle_righ.description: The digastric muscle (also digastricus) (named digastric as it has two 'bellies') is a small muscle located under the jaw. The term "digastric muscle" refers to this specific muscle. However, other muscles that have two separate muscle bellies include the suspensory muscle of duodenum, omohyoid, occipitofrontalis.

posterior_cerebral_artery_left.name: Posterior cerebral artery (left)
posterior_cerebral_artery_left.description: The posterior cerebral artery (PCA) is one of a pair of cerebral arteries that supply oxygenated blood to the occipital lobe, part of the back of the human brain. The two arteries originate from the distal end of the basilar artery, where it bifurcates into the left and right posterior cerebral arteries.

posterior_cerebral_artery_right.name: Posterior cerebral artery (right)
posterior_cerebral_artery_right.description: The posterior cerebral artery (PCA) is one of a pair of cerebral arteries that supply oxygenated blood to the occipital lobe, part of the back of the human brain. The two arteries originate from the distal end of the basilar artery, where it bifurcates into the left and right posterior cerebral arteries.

posterior_cochlear_nucleus_left.name: Posterior cochlear nucleus (left)
posterior_cochlear_nucleus_left.description: The cochlear nuclear (CN) complex comprises two cranial nerve nuclei in the human brainstem, the ventral cochlear nucleus (VCN) and the dorsal cochlear nucleus (DCN). The ventral (anterior) cochlear nucleus is unlayered whereas the dorsal cochlear nucleus is layered.

posterior_cochlear_nucleus_right.name: Posterior cochlear nucleus (right)
posterior_cochlear_nucleus_right.description: The cochlear nuclear (CN) complex comprises two cranial nerve nuclei in the human brainstem, the ventral cochlear nucleus (VCN) and the dorsal cochlear nucleus (DCN). The ventral (anterior) cochlear nucleus is unlayered whereas the dorsal cochlear nucleus is layered.

posterior_commissure.name: Posterior commissure
posterior_commissure.description: The posterior commissure (also known as the epithalamic commissure) is a rounded band of white fibers crossing the middle line on the dorsal aspect of the rostral end of the cerebral aqueduct. It is important in the bilateral pupillary light reflex.

posterior_communicating_artery_left.name: Posterior communicating artery (left)
posterior_communicating_artery_left.description: In human anatomy, the left and right posterior communicating arteries are arteries at the base of the brain that form part of the circle of Willis. Each posterior communicating artery connects the three cerebral arteries of the same side.

posterior_communicating_artery_right.name: Posterior communicating artery (right)
posterior_communicating_artery_right.description: In human anatomy, the left and right posterior communicating arteries are arteries at the base of the brain that form part of the circle of Willis. Each posterior communicating artery connects the three cerebral arteries of the same side.

posterior_division_of_mandibular_nerve_l.name: Posterior division of mandibular nerve (left)
posterior_division_of_mandibular_nerve_l.description: The mandibular nerve divides into a small anterior and large posterior trunk after passing between tensor veli palatini, which is medial, and lateral pterygoid, which is lateral, and giving off a meningeal branch (nervus spinosus) and the nerve to medial pterygoid from its medial side.

posterior_division_of_mandibular_nerve_r.name: Posterior division of mandibular nerve (right)
posterior_division_of_mandibular_nerve_r.description: The mandibular nerve divides into a small anterior and large posterior trunk after passing between tensor veli palatini, which is medial, and lateral pterygoid, which is lateral, and giving off a meningeal branch (nervus spinosus) and the nerve to medial pterygoid from its medial side.

posterior_division_of_retromandibular_ve.name: Posterior division of retromandibular vein (left)
posterior_division_of_retromandibular_ve.description: The retromandibular vein (temporomaxillary vein, posterior facial vein) is a major vein of the face.

posterior_division_of_retromandibular_ve.name: Posterior division of retromandibular vein (right)
posterior_division_of_retromandibular_ve.description: The retromandibular vein (temporomaxillary vein, posterior facial vein) is a major vein of the face.

posterior_ethmoidal_artery_left.name: Posterior ethmoidal artery (left)
posterior_ethmoidal_artery_left.description: The posterior ethmoidal artery is an artery of the head which supplies the nasal septum. It is smaller than the anterior ethmoidal artery.

posterior_ethmoidal_artery_right.name: Posterior ethmoidal artery (right)
posterior_ethmoidal_artery_right.description: The posterior ethmoidal artery is an artery of the head which supplies the nasal septum. It is smaller than the anterior ethmoidal artery.

posterior_inferior_cerebellar_artery_lef.name: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (left)
posterior_inferior_cerebellar_artery_lef.description: The posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) is the largest branch of the vertebral artery. It is one of the three main arteries that supply blood to the cerebellum, a part of the brain. Blockage of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery can result in a type of stroke called lateral medullary syndrome.

posterior_inferior_cerebellar_artery_rig.name: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (right)
posterior_inferior_cerebellar_artery_rig.description: The posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) is the largest branch of the vertebral artery. It is one of the three main arteries that supply blood to the cerebellum, a part of the brain. Blockage of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery can result in a type of stroke called lateral medullary syndrome.

posterior_intercavernous_sinus.name: Posterior intercavernous sinus
posterior_intercavernous_sinus.description: The intercavernous sinuses are two in number, an anterior and a posterior, and connect the two cavernous sinuses[1] across the middle line.

posterior_lateral_nasal_branches_of_sphe.name: Posterior lateral nasal branches of sphenopalatine artery. (left)
Posterior lateral nasal branches of sphenopalatine artery. (right)

posterior_nucleus_of_vagus_nerve_left.name: Posterior nucleus of vagus nerve (left)
posterior_nucleus_of_vagus_nerve_left.description: The dorsal nucleus of vagus nerve (or posterior nucleus of vagus nerve or dorsal vagal nucleus or nucleus dorsalis nervi vagi or nucleus posterior nervi vagi) is a cranial nerve nucleus for the vagus nerve in the medulla that lies ventral to the floor of the fourth ventricle.

posterior_nucleus_of_vagus_nerve_right.name: Posterior nucleus of vagus nerve (right)
posterior_nucleus_of_vagus_nerve_right.description: The dorsal nucleus of vagus nerve (or posterior nucleus of vagus nerve or dorsal vagal nucleus or nucleus dorsalis nervi vagi or nucleus posterior nervi vagi) is a cranial nerve nucleus for the vagus nerve in the medulla that lies ventral to the floor of the fourth ventricle.

posterior_region_of_neck_left.name: Posterior region of neck (left)
posterior_region_of_neck_left.description: Covers the ascending part of trapezius muscle.

posterior_region_of_neck_right.name: Posterior region of neck (right)
posterior_region_of_neck_right.description: Covers the ascending part of trapezius muscle.

posterior_segment_of_eyeball_left.name: Posterior segment of eyeball (left)
posterior_segment_of_eyeball_left.description: The posterior segment or posterior cavity is the back two-thirds of the eye that includes the anterior hyaloid membrane and all of the optical structures behind it: the vitreous humor, retina, choroid, and optic nerve.

posterior_segment_of_eyeball_right.name: Posterior segment of eyeball (right)
posterior_segment_of_eyeball_right.description: The posterior segment or posterior cavity is the back two-thirds of the eye that includes the anterior hyaloid membrane and all of the optical structures behind it: the vitreous humor, retina, choroid, and optic nerve.

posterior_septal_branches_of_sphenopalat.name: Posterior septal branches of sphenopalatine artery (left)
posterior_septal_branches_of_sphenopalat.description: Crossing the under surface of the sphenoid the sphenopalatine artery ends on the nasal septum as the posterior septal branches; these anastomose with the ethmoidal arteries and the septal branch of the superior labial; one branch descends in a groove on the vomer to the incisive canal and anastomoses with the descending palatine artery.

posterior_septal_branches_of_sphenopalat.name: Posterior septal branches of sphenopalatine artery (right)
posterior_septal_branches_of_sphenopalat.description: Crossing the under surface of the sphenoid the sphenopalatine artery ends on the nasal septum as the posterior septal branches; these anastomose with the ethmoidal arteries and the septal branch of the superior labial; one branch descends in a groove on the vomer to the incisive canal and anastomoses with the descending palatine artery.

posterior_superior_alveolar_artery_left.name: Posterior superior alveolar artery (left)
posterior_superior_alveolar_artery_left.description: The posterior superior alveolar artery (posterior dental artery) is given off from the maxillary, frequently in conjunction with the infraorbital artery just as the trunk of the vessel is passing into the pterygopalatine fossa.

posterior_superior_alveolar_artery_right.name: Posterior superior alveolar artery (right)
posterior_superior_alveolar_artery_right.description: The posterior superior alveolar artery (posterior dental artery) is given off from the maxillary, frequently in conjunction with the infraorbital artery just as the trunk of the vessel is passing into the pterygopalatine fossa.

precentral_gyrus_left.name: Precentral gyrus (left)
precentral_gyrus_left.description: The precentral gyrus is a prominent gyrus on the surface of the posterior frontal lobe of the brain. It is the site of the primary motor cortex that in humans is cytoarchitecturally defined as Brodmann area 4.

precentral_gyrus_right.name: Precentral gyrus (right)
precentral_gyrus_right.description: The precentral gyrus is a prominent gyrus on the surface of the posterior frontal lobe of the brain. It is the site of the primary motor cortex that in humans is cytoarchitecturally defined as Brodmann area 4.

precentral_sulcus_inferior_part_left.name: Precentral sulcus (inferior part)* (left)
precentral_sulcus_inferior_part_left.description: The precentral sulcus is a part of the human brain that lies parallel to, and in front of, the central sulcus. (A sulcus is one of the prominent grooves on the surface of the human brain.) The precentral sulcus divides the inferior, middle and superior frontal gyri from the precentral gyrus.

precentral_sulcus_inferior_part_right.name: Precentral sulcus (inferior part)* (right)
precentral_sulcus_inferior_part_right.description: The precentral sulcus is a part of the human brain that lies parallel to, and in front of, the central sulcus. (A sulcus is one of the prominent grooves on the surface of the human brain.) The precentral sulcus divides the inferior, middle and superior frontal gyri from the precentral gyrus.

precentral_sulcus_superior_part_left.name: Precentral sulcus (Superior part)* (left)
precentral_sulcus_superior_part_left.description: The precentral sulcus is a part of the human brain that lies parallel to, and in front of, the central sulcus. (A sulcus is one of the prominent grooves on the surface of the human brain.) The precentral sulcus divides the inferior, middle and superior frontal gyri from the precentral gyrus.

precentral_sulcus_superior_part_right.name: Precentral sulcus (Superior part)* (right)
precentral_sulcus_superior_part_right.description: The precentral sulcus is a part of the human brain that lies parallel to, and in front of, the central sulcus. (A sulcus is one of the prominent grooves on the surface of the human brain.) The precentral sulcus divides the inferior, middle and superior frontal gyri from the precentral gyrus.

precuneus_left.name: Precuneus (left)
precuneus_left.description: The precuneus is the portion of the superior parietal lobule on the medial surface of each brain hemisphere. It is located in front of the cuneus (the upper portion of the occipital lobe).

precuneus_right.name: Precuneus (right)
precuneus_right.description: The precuneus is the portion of the superior parietal lobule on the medial surface of each brain hemisphere. It is located in front of the cuneus (the upper portion of the occipital lobe).

procerus_muscle_left.name: Procerus muscle (left)
procerus_muscle_left.description: The procerus muscle (or pyramidalis nasi) is a small pyramidal slip of muscle deep to the superior orbital nerve, artery and vein. Procerus is Latin, meaning tall or extended.

procerus_muscle_right.name: Procerus muscle (right)
procerus_muscle_right.description: The procerus muscle (or pyramidalis nasi) is a small pyramidal slip of muscle deep to the superior orbital nerve, artery and vein. Procerus is Latin, meaning tall or extended.

putamen_left.name: Putamen (left)
putamen_left.description: The putamen (; from Latin, meaning "nutshell") is a round structure located at the base of the forebrain (telencephalon). The putamen and caudate nucleus together form the dorsal striatum. It is also one of the structures that compose the basal nuclei.

putamen_right.name: Putamen (right)
putamen_right.description: The putamen (; from Latin, meaning "nutshell") is a round structure located at the base of the forebrain (telencephalon). The putamen and caudate nucleus together form the dorsal striatum. It is also one of the structures that compose the basal nuclei.

pyramid_of_medulla_oblongata_left.name: Pyramid of medulla oblongata (left)
pyramid_of_medulla_oblongata_left.description: The medullary pyramids are paired white matter structures of the brainstem's medulla oblongata that contain motor fibers of the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts – known together as the pyramidal tracts. The lower limit of the pyramids is marked when the fibers cross (decussate).

pyramid_of_medulla_oblongata_right.name: Pyramid of medulla oblongata (right)
pyramid_of_medulla_oblongata_right.description: The medullary pyramids are paired white matter structures of the brainstem's medulla oblongata that contain motor fibers of the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts – known together as the pyramidal tracts. The lower limit of the pyramids is marked when the fibers cross (decussate).

quadrangular_membrane_left.name: Quadrangular membrane (left)
quadrangular_membrane_left.description: The quadrangular membrane is a layer of submucosa. It contains the cuneiform cartilages. The membrane runs between the lateral aspects of the epiglottis and arytenoid cartilages on each side. The free inferior border of the quadrangular membrane is the vestibular fold which is the vestibular ligament when covered by mucosa.

quadrangular_membrane_right.name: Quadrangular membrane (right)
quadrangular_membrane_right.description: The quadrangular membrane is a layer of submucosa. It contains the cuneiform cartilages. The membrane runs between the lateral aspects of the epiglottis and arytenoid cartilages on each side. The free inferior border of the quadrangular membrane is the vestibular fold which is the vestibular ligament when covered by mucosa.

rectus_posterior_major_capitis_muscle_le.name: Rectus posterior major capitis muscle (left)
rectus_posterior_major_capitis_muscle_le.description: The rectus capitis posterior major (or rectus capitis posticus major, both being Latin for larger posterior straight muscle of the head) arises by a pointed tendon from the spinous process of the axis, and, becoming broader as it ascends, is inserted into the lateral part of the inferior nuchal line of the occipital bone and the surface of the bone immediately below the line.

rectus_posterior_major_capitis_muscle_ri.name: Rectus posterior major capitis muscle (right)
rectus_posterior_major_capitis_muscle_ri.description: The rectus capitis posterior major (or rectus capitis posticus major, both being Latin for larger posterior straight muscle of the head) arises by a pointed tendon from the spinous process of the axis, and, becoming broader as it ascends, is inserted into the lateral part of the inferior nuchal line of the occipital bone and the surface of the bone immediately below the line.

rectus_posterior_minor_capitis_muscle_le.name: Rectus posterior minor capitis muscle (left)
rectus_posterior_minor_capitis_muscle_le.description: The rectus posterior minor capitis minor arises by a narrow pointed tendon from the tubercle on the posterior arch of the atlas, and, widening as it ascends, is inserted into the medial part of the inferior nuchal line of the occipital bone and the surface between it and the foramen magnum, and also takes some attachment to the spinal dura mater.

rectus_posterior_minor_capitis_muscle_ri.name: Rectus posterior minor capitis muscle (right)
rectus_posterior_minor_capitis_muscle_ri.description: The rectus posterior minor capitis minor arises by a narrow pointed tendon from the tubercle on the posterior arch of the atlas, and, widening as it ascends, is inserted into the medial part of the inferior nuchal line of the occipital bone and the surface between it and the foramen magnum, and also takes some attachment to the spinal dura mater.

red_nucleus_left.name: Red nucleus (left)
red_nucleus_left.description: The red nucleus or nucleus ruber is a structure in the rostral midbrain involved in motor coordination. The red nucleus is pale pink, which is believed to be due to the presence of iron in at least two different forms: hemoglobin and ferritin.

red_nucleus_right.name: Red nucleus (right)
red_nucleus_right.description: The red nucleus or nucleus ruber is a structure in the rostral midbrain involved in motor coordination. The red nucleus is pale pink, which is believed to be due to the presence of iron in at least two different forms: hemoglobin and ferritin.

retina_left.name: Retina (left)
retina_left.description: The retina (from Latin: rete "net") is the innermost, light-sensitive layer of tissue of the eye of most vertebrates and some molluscs. The optics of the eye create a focused two-dimensional image of the visual world on the retina, which translates that image into electrical neural impulses to the brain to create visual perception.

retina_right.name: Retina (right)
retina_right.description: The retina (from Latin: rete "net") is the innermost, light-sensitive layer of tissue of the eye of most vertebrates and some molluscs. The optics of the eye create a focused two-dimensional image of the visual world on the retina, which translates that image into electrical neural impulses to the brain to create visual perception.

retromandibular_vein_left.name: Retromandibular vein (left)
retromandibular_vein_left.description: The retromandibular vein (temporomaxillary vein, posterior facial vein) is a major vein of the face.

retromandibular_vein_right.name: Retromandibular vein (right)
retromandibular_vein_right.description: The retromandibular vein (temporomaxillary vein, posterior facial vein) is a major vein of the face.

retropharyngeal_nodes_left.name: Retropharyngeal nodes (left)
retropharyngeal_nodes_left.description: The retropharyngeal lymph nodes, from one to three in number, lie in the buccopharyngeal fascia, behind the upper part of the pharynx and in front of the arch of the atlas, being separated, however, from the latter by the Longus capitis. Their afferents drain the nasal cavities, the nasal part of the pharynx, and the auditory tubes.

retropharyngeal_nodes_right.name: Retropharyngeal nodes (right)
retropharyngeal_nodes_right.description: The retropharyngeal lymph nodes, from one to three in number, lie in the buccopharyngeal fascia, behind the upper part of the pharynx and in front of the arch of the atlas, being separated, however, from the latter by the Longus capitis. Their afferents drain the nasal cavities, the nasal part of the pharynx, and the auditory tubes.

risorius_muscle_left.name: Risorius muscle (left)
risorius_muscle_left.description: The risorius muscle is a muscle of facial expression. It arises from the fascia over the parotid gland, and inserts into the angle of the mouth. It is supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII). It may be absent or asymmetrical in some people. It retracts the angle of the mouth during smiling.

risorius_muscle_right.name: Risorius muscle (right)
risorius_muscle_right.description: The risorius muscle is a muscle of facial expression. It arises from the fascia over the parotid gland, and inserts into the angle of the mouth. It is supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII). It may be absent or asymmetrical in some people. It retracts the angle of the mouth during smiling.

scapha_left.name: Scapha (left)
scapha_left.description: The depression or groove between the helix and the antihelix.

scapha_right.name: Scapha (right)
scapha_right.description: The depression or groove between the helix and the antihelix.

sclera_left.name: Sclera (left)
sclera_left.description: The sclera, also known as the white of the eye or, in older literature, as the tunica albuginea oculi, is the opaque, fibrous, protective, outer layer of the human eye containing mainly collagen and some crucial elastic fiber.

sclera_right.name: Sclera (right)
sclera_right.description: The sclera, also known as the white of the eye or, in older literature, as the tunica albuginea oculi, is the opaque, fibrous, protective, outer layer of the human eye containing mainly collagen and some crucial elastic fiber.

sensory_root_of_trigeminal_nerve_left.name: Sensory root of trigeminal nerve (left)
sensory_root_of_trigeminal_nerve_left.description: The principal sensory nucleus of trigeminal nerve (or chief sensory nucleus of V, main trigeminal sensory nucleus) is a group of second-order neurons which have cell bodies in the caudal pons.

sensory_root_of_trigeminal_nerve_right.name: Sensory root of trigeminal nerve (right)
sensory_root_of_trigeminal_nerve_right.description: The principal sensory nucleus of trigeminal nerve (or chief sensory nucleus of V, main trigeminal sensory nucleus) is a group of second-order neurons which have cell bodies in the caudal pons.

septal_branches_of_posterior_ethmoidal_a.name: Septal branches of posterior ethmoidal artery (left)
Septal branches of posterior ethmoidal artery (right)

septal_nuclei.name: Septal nuclei
septal_nuclei.description: The septal area (medial olfactory area), consisting of the lateral septum and medial septum, is an area in the lower, posterior part of the medial surface of the frontal lobe, and refers to the nearby septum pellucidum. The septal nuclei are located in this area.

septum_pellucidum.name: Septum pellucidum
septum_pellucidum.description: The septum pellucidum (Latin for "translucent wall") is a thin, triangular, vertical double membrane separating the anterior horns of the left and right lateral ventricles of the brain. It runs as a sheet from the corpus callosum down to the fornix. The septum is not present in the syndrome septo-optic dysplasia.

sigmoid_sinus_left.name: Sigmoid sinus (left)
sigmoid_sinus_left.description: The sigmoid sinuses (sigma- or s-shaped hollow curve), also known as the pars sigmoid, are venous sinuses within the skull that receive blood from posterior dural venous sinus veins.

sigmoid_sinus_right.name: Sigmoid sinus (right)
sigmoid_sinus_right.description: The sigmoid sinuses (sigma- or s-shaped hollow curve), also known as the pars sigmoid, are venous sinuses within the skull that receive blood from posterior dural venous sinus veins.

sinus_of_frontal_bone.name: Sinus of frontal bone
sinus_of_frontal_bone.description: The frontal sinuses are one of the four pairs of paranasal sinuses that are situated behind the brow ridges. Sinuses are mucosa-lined airspaces within the bones of the face and skull.

sinus_of_sphenoid_bone.name: Sinus of sphenoid bone
sinus_of_sphenoid_bone.description: The sphenoid sinus is one of the four paired paranasal sinuses that is contained within the body of the sphenoid bone. The sphenoid sinuses vary in size and shape, and owing to the lateral displacement of the intervening septum, which may insert on the carotid canal, they are rarely symmetrical.

soft_palate.name: Soft palate
soft_palate.description: The soft palate (also known as the velum, palatal velum, or muscular palate) is, in mammals, the soft tissue constituting the back of the roof of the mouth. The soft palate is part of the palate of the mouth; the other part is the hard palate.

sphenoid_bone.name: Sphenoid bone
sphenoid_bone.description: The sphenoid bone is an unpaired bone of the neurocranium. It is situated in the middle of the skull towards the front, in front of the basilar part of the occipital bone. The sphenoid bone is one of the seven bones that articulate to form the orbit. Its shape somewhat resembles that of a butterfly or bat with its wings extended.

sphenomandibular_ligament_left.name: Sphenomandibular ligament (left)
sphenomandibular_ligament_left.description: The sphenomandibular ligament (internal lateral ligament) is a flat, thin band which is attached superiorly to the spina angularis (spine) of the sphenoid bone, and, becoming broader as it descends, is fixed to the lingula of the mandibular foramen.

sphenomandibular_ligament_right.name: Sphenomandibular ligament (right)
sphenomandibular_ligament_right.description: The sphenomandibular ligament (internal lateral ligament) is a flat, thin band which is attached superiorly to the spina angularis (spine) of the sphenoid bone, and, becoming broader as it descends, is fixed to the lingula of the mandibular foramen.

spinalis_capitis_muscle_left.name: Spinalis capitis muscle (left)
spinalis_capitis_muscle_left.description: Spinalis capitis (biventer cervicis) is usually inseparably connected with the semispinalis capitis. Spinalis capitis is not well characterized in modern anatomy textbooks and atlases, and is often omitted from anatomical illustration.

spinalis_capitis_muscle_right.name: Spinalis capitis muscle (right)
spinalis_capitis_muscle_right.description: Spinalis capitis (biventer cervicis) is usually inseparably connected with the semispinalis capitis. Spinalis capitis is not well characterized in modern anatomy textbooks and atlases, and is often omitted from anatomical illustration.

sternocleidomastoid_region_left.name: Sternocleidomastoid region (left)
sternocleidomastoid_region_left.description: It corresponds to the sternocleidomastoid muscle.

sternocleidomastoid_region_right.name: Sternocleidomastoid region (right)
sternocleidomastoid_region_right.description: It corresponds to the sternocleidomastoid muscle.

straight_gyrus_gyrus_rectus_left.name: Straight gyrus (Gyrus rectus) (left)
straight_gyrus_gyrus_rectus_left.description: The portion of the inferior frontal lobe immediately adjacent to the longitudinal fissure (and medial to the medial orbital gyrus and olfactory tract) is named the straight gyrus,(or gyrus rectus) and is continuous with the superior frontal gyrus on the medial surface.

straight_gyrus_gyrus_rectus_right.name: Straight gyrus (Gyrus rectus) (right)
straight_gyrus_gyrus_rectus_right.description: The portion of the inferior frontal lobe immediately adjacent to the longitudinal fissure (and medial to the medial orbital gyrus and olfactory tract) is named the straight gyrus,(or gyrus rectus) and is continuous with the superior frontal gyrus on the medial surface.

straight_sinus.name: Straight sinus
straight_sinus.description: The straight sinus, also known as tentorial sinus or the sinus rectus, is an area within the skull beneath the brain. It receives blood from the inferior sagittal sinus and the great cerebral vein, and drains into the confluence of sinuses.

stria_medullaris_thalami_left.name: Stria medullaris thalami (left)
stria_medullaris_thalami_left.description: The stria medullaris is a part of the epithalamus. It is a fiber bundle containing afferent fibers from the septal nuclei, lateral preoptico-hypothalamic region, and anterior thalamic nuclei to the habenula.

stria_medullaris_thalami_right.name: Stria medullaris thalami (right)
stria_medullaris_thalami_right.description: The stria medullaris is a part of the epithalamus. It is a fiber bundle containing afferent fibers from the septal nuclei, lateral preoptico-hypothalamic region, and anterior thalamic nuclei to the habenula.

stria_terminalis_left.name: Stria terminalis (left)
stria_terminalis_left.description: The stria terminalis (or terminal stria) is a structure in the brain consisting of a band of fibers running along the lateral margin of the ventricular surface of the thalamus. Serving as a major output pathway of the amygdala, the stria terminalis runs from its centromedial division to the ventromedial nucleus of the hypothalamus.

stria_terminalis_right.name: Stria terminalis (right)
stria_terminalis_right.description: The stria terminalis (or terminal stria) is a structure in the brain consisting of a band of fibers running along the lateral margin of the ventricular surface of the thalamus. Serving as a major output pathway of the amygdala, the stria terminalis runs from its centromedial division to the ventromedial nucleus of the hypothalamus.

stylohyoid_ligament_left.name: Stylohyoid ligament (left)
stylohyoid_ligament_left.description: The stylohyoid ligament is a ligament that connects the hyoid bone to the temporal styloid process (of the temporal bone of the skull).

stylohyoid_ligament_right.name: Stylohyoid ligament (right)
stylohyoid_ligament_right.description: The stylohyoid ligament is a ligament that connects the hyoid bone to the temporal styloid process (of the temporal bone of the skull).

stylohyoid_muscle_left.name: Stylohyoid muscle (left)
stylohyoid_muscle_left.description: The stylohyoid muscle is a slender muscle, lying anterior and superior of the posterior belly of the digastric muscle. It is one of the suprahyoid muscles. It shares this muscle's innervation by the facial nerve, and functions to draw the hyoid bone backwards and elevate the tongue. Its origin is the styloid process of the temporal bone.

stylohyoid_muscle_right.name: Stylohyoid muscle (right)
stylohyoid_muscle_right.description: The stylohyoid muscle is a slender muscle, lying anterior and superior of the posterior belly of the digastric muscle. It is one of the suprahyoid muscles. It shares this muscle's innervation by the facial nerve, and functions to draw the hyoid bone backwards and elevate the tongue. Its origin is the styloid process of the temporal bone.

stylomandibular_ligament_left.name: Stylomandibular ligament (left)
stylomandibular_ligament_left.description: The stylomandibular ligament is the thickened posterior portion of the investing cervical fascia around the neck. It extends from near the apex of the styloid process of the temporal bone to the angle and posterior border of the angle of the mandible, between the masseter muscle and medial pterygoid muscle.

stylomandibular_ligament_right.name: Stylomandibular ligament (right)
stylomandibular_ligament_right.description: The stylomandibular ligament is the thickened posterior portion of the investing cervical fascia around the neck. It extends from near the apex of the styloid process of the temporal bone to the angle and posterior border of the angle of the mandible, between the masseter muscle and medial pterygoid muscle.

stylopharyngeus_muscle_left.name: Stylopharyngeus muscle (left)
stylopharyngeus_muscle_left.description: The stylopharyngeus is a muscle in the head that stretches between the temporal styloid process and the pharynx.

stylopharyngeus_muscle_right.name: Stylopharyngeus muscle (right)
stylopharyngeus_muscle_right.description: The stylopharyngeus is a muscle in the head that stretches between the temporal styloid process and the pharynx.

sublingual_gland_left.name: Sublingual gland (left)
sublingual_gland_left.description: The paired sublingual glands are major salivary glands in the mouth. They are the smallest, most diffuse, and the only unencapsulated major salivary glands. They provide only 3-5% of the total salivary volume. There are also two other types of salivary glands; they are submandibular and parotid glands.

sublingual_gland_right.name: Sublingual gland (right)
sublingual_gland_right.description: The paired sublingual glands are major salivary glands in the mouth. They are the smallest, most diffuse, and the only unencapsulated major salivary glands. They provide only 3-5% of the total salivary volume. There are also two other types of salivary glands; they are submandibular and parotid glands.

submandibular_duct_left.name: Submandibular duct (left)
submandibular_duct_left.description: The submandibular duct or Wharton duct or submaxillary duct, is one of the salivary excretory ducts. It is about 5 cm. long, and its wall is much thinner than that of the parotid duct. It drains saliva from each bilateral submandibular gland and sublingual gland to the sublingual caruncle at the base of the tongue.

submandibular_duct_right.name: Submandibular duct (right)
submandibular_duct_right.description: The submandibular duct or Wharton duct or submaxillary duct, is one of the salivary excretory ducts. It is about 5 cm. long, and its wall is much thinner than that of the parotid duct. It drains saliva from each bilateral submandibular gland and sublingual gland to the sublingual caruncle at the base of the tongue.

submandibular_gland_left.name: Submandibular gland (left)
submandibular_gland_left.description: The paired submandibular glands (historically known as submaxillary glands) are major salivary glands located beneath the floor of the mouth. They each weigh about 15 grams and contribute some 60–67% of unstimulated saliva secretion; on stimulation their contribution decreases in proportion as the parotid secretion rises to 50%.

submandibular_gland_right.name: Submandibular gland (right)
submandibular_gland_right.description: The paired submandibular glands (historically known as submaxillary glands) are major salivary glands located beneath the floor of the mouth. They each weigh about 15 grams and contribute some 60–67% of unstimulated saliva secretion; on stimulation their contribution decreases in proportion as the parotid secretion rises to 50%.

submandibular_nodes_left.name: Submandibular nodes (left)
submandibular_nodes_left.description: The submandibular lymph nodes (submaxillary glands in older texts), three to six in number, are lymph nodes beneath the body of the mandible in the submandibular triangle, and rest on the superficial surface of the submandibular gland.

submandibular_nodes_right.name: Submandibular nodes (right)
submandibular_nodes_right.description: The submandibular lymph nodes (submaxillary glands in older texts), three to six in number, are lymph nodes beneath the body of the mandible in the submandibular triangle, and rest on the superficial surface of the submandibular gland.

submandibular_triangle_left.name: Submandibular triangle (left)
submandibular_triangle_left.description: The submandibular triangle (or submaxillary or digastric triangle) corresponds to the region of the neck immediately beneath the body of the mandible.

submandibular_triangle_right.name: Submandibular triangle (right)
submandibular_triangle_right.description: The submandibular triangle (or submaxillary or digastric triangle) corresponds to the region of the neck immediately beneath the body of the mandible.

submental_artery_left.name: Submental artery (left)
submental_artery_left.description: The submental artery is a branch of the facial artery that runs on the underside of the chin.

submental_artery_right.name: Submental artery (right)
submental_artery_right.description: The submental artery is a branch of the facial artery that runs on the underside of the chin.

submental_nodes_left.name: Submental nodes (left)
submental_nodes_left.description: The submental glands (or suprahyoid) are situated between the anterior bellies of the digastric muscle and the hyoid bone. Their afferents drain the central portions of the lower lip and floor of the mouth and the apex of the tongue.

submental_nodes_right.name: Submental nodes (right)
submental_nodes_right.description: The submental glands (or suprahyoid) are situated between the anterior bellies of the digastric muscle and the hyoid bone. Their afferents drain the central portions of the lower lip and floor of the mouth and the apex of the tongue.

submental_triangle_left.name: Submental triangle (left)
submental_triangle_left.description: The submental triangle (or suprahyoid triangle) is a division of the anterior triangle of the neck.

submental_triangle_right.name: Submental triangle (right)
submental_triangle_right.description: The submental triangle (or suprahyoid triangle) is a division of the anterior triangle of the neck.

submental_vein_left.name: Submental vein (left)
submental_vein_left.description: Following the submental artery, the submental vein anastomoses with the sublingual vein and the anterior jugular vein.

submental_vein_right.name: Submental vein (right)
submental_vein_right.description: Following the submental artery, the submental vein anastomoses with the sublingual vein and the anterior jugular vein.

subparietal_sulcus_left.name: Subparietal sulcus (left)
subparietal_sulcus_left.description: The subparietal sulcus (Sulcus subparietalis) or suprasplenial sulcus is a sulcus, or crevice, on the medial surface of each cerebral hemisphere, above the splenium of the corpus callosum. It separates the precuneus from the posterior part of the cingulate gyrus. It is the posterior continuation of the cingulate sulcus.

subparietal_sulcus_right.name: Subparietal sulcus (right)
subparietal_sulcus_right.description: The subparietal sulcus (Sulcus subparietalis) or suprasplenial sulcus is a sulcus, or crevice, on the medial surface of each cerebral hemisphere, above the splenium of the corpus callosum. It separates the precuneus from the posterior part of the cingulate gyrus. It is the posterior continuation of the cingulate sulcus.

superficial_part_of_masseter_left.name: Superficial part of masseter (left)
superficial_part_of_masseter_left.description: In human anatomy, the masseter is one of the muscles of mastication. Found only in mammals, it is particularly powerful in herbivores to facilitate chewing of plant matter. The most obvious muscle of mastication is the masseter muscle, since it is the most superficial and one of the strongest.

superficial_part_of_masseter_right.name: Superficial part of masseter (right)
superficial_part_of_masseter_right.description: In human anatomy, the masseter is one of the muscles of mastication. Found only in mammals, it is particularly powerful in herbivores to facilitate chewing of plant matter. The most obvious muscle of mastication is the masseter muscle, since it is the most superficial and one of the strongest.

superficial_temporal_artery_left.name: Superficial temporal artery (left)
superficial_temporal_artery_left.description: In human anatomy, the superficial temporal artery is a major artery of the head. It arises from the external carotid artery when it splits into the superficial temporal artery and maxillary artery. Its pulse can be felt above the zygomatic arch, above and in front of the tragus of the ear.

superficial_temporal_artery_right.name: Superficial temporal artery (right)
superficial_temporal_artery_right.description: In human anatomy, the superficial temporal artery is a major artery of the head. It arises from the external carotid artery when it splits into the superficial temporal artery and maxillary artery. Its pulse can be felt above the zygomatic arch, above and in front of the tragus of the ear.

superficial_temporal_veins_left.name: Superficial temporal veins (left)
superficial_temporal_veins_left.description: The superficial temporal vein is a vein of the side of the head. It begins on the side and vertex of the skull in a network of veins which communicates with the frontal vein and supraorbital vein, with the corresponding vein of the opposite side, and with the posterior auricular vein and occipital vein.

superficial_temporal_veins_right.name: Superficial temporal veins (right)
superficial_temporal_veins_right.description: The superficial temporal vein is a vein of the side of the head. It begins on the side and vertex of the skull in a network of veins which communicates with the frontal vein and supraorbital vein, with the corresponding vein of the opposite side, and with the posterior auricular vein and occipital vein.

superior_cerebellar_artery_left.name: Superior cerebellar artery (left)
superior_cerebellar_artery_left.description: The superior cerebellar artery (SCA) is an artery of the head. It arises near the end of the basilar artery. It is a branch of the basilar artery. It supplies parts of the cerebellum, the midbrain, and other nearby structures. It is the cause of trigeminal neuralgia in some patients.

superior_cerebellar_artery_right.name: Superior cerebellar artery (right)
superior_cerebellar_artery_right.description: The superior cerebellar artery (SCA) is an artery of the head. It arises near the end of the basilar artery. It is a branch of the basilar artery. It supplies parts of the cerebellum, the midbrain, and other nearby structures. It is the cause of trigeminal neuralgia in some patients.

superior_cerebellar_peduncle_left.name: Superior cerebellar peduncle (left)
superior_cerebellar_peduncle_left.description: In the human brain, the superior cerebellar peduncle (brachium conjunctivum) is a paired structure of white matter that connects the cerebellum to the midbrain.

superior_cerebellar_peduncle_right.name: Superior cerebellar peduncle (right)
superior_cerebellar_peduncle_right.description: In the human brain, the superior cerebellar peduncle (brachium conjunctivum) is a paired structure of white matter that connects the cerebellum to the midbrain.

superior_colliculus_left.name: Superior colliculus (left)
superior_colliculus_left.description: The superior colliculus (Latin for upper hill) is a structure lying on the roof of the mammalian midbrain. In non-mammalian vertebrates, the homologous structure is known as the optic tectum, or optic lobe. The adjective form tectal is commonly used for both structures.

superior_colliculus_right.name: Superior colliculus (right)
superior_colliculus_right.description: The superior colliculus (Latin for upper hill) is a structure lying on the roof of the mammalian midbrain. In non-mammalian vertebrates, the homologous structure is known as the optic tectum, or optic lobe. The adjective form tectal is commonly used for both structures.

superior_frontal_gyrus_left.name: Superior frontal gyrus (left)
superior_frontal_gyrus_left.description: The superior frontal gyrus (SFG) also marginal gyrus, makes up about one third of the frontal lobe of the human brain. It is bounded laterally by the superior frontal sulcus.The superior frontal gyrus is one of the frontal gyri.

superior_frontal_gyrus_right.name: Superior frontal gyrus (right)
superior_frontal_gyrus_right.description: The superior frontal gyrus (SFG) also marginal gyrus, makes up about one third of the frontal lobe of the human brain. It is bounded laterally by the superior frontal sulcus.The superior frontal gyrus is one of the frontal gyri.

superior_frontal_sulcus_left.name: Superior frontal sulcus (left)
superior_frontal_sulcus_left.description: The superior frontal sulcus is a sulcus between the superior frontal gyrus and the middle frontal gyrus. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superior_frontal_sulcus

superior_frontal_sulcus_right.name: Superior frontal sulcus (right)
superior_frontal_sulcus_right.description: The superior frontal sulcus is a sulcus between the superior frontal gyrus and the middle frontal gyrus. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superior_frontal_sulcus

superior_head_of_lateral_pterygoid_muscl.name: Superior head of lateral pterygoid muscle (left)
superior_head_of_lateral_pterygoid_muscl.description: The lateral pterygoid or external pterygoid is a muscle of mastication with two heads. It lies superiorly to the medial pterygoid.

superior_head_of_lateral_pterygoid_muscl.name: Superior head of lateral pterygoid muscle (right)
superior_head_of_lateral_pterygoid_muscl.description: The lateral pterygoid or external pterygoid is a muscle of mastication with two heads. It lies superiorly to the medial pterygoid.

superior_labial_artery_left.name: Superior labial artery (left)
superior_labial_artery_left.description: The superior labial artery (superior labial branch of facial artery) is larger and more egregious than the inferior labial artery. It follows a similar course along the edge of the upper lip, lying between the mucous membrane and the orbicularis oris, and anastomoses with the artery of the opposite side.

superior_labial_artery_right.name: Superior labial artery (right)
superior_labial_artery_right.description: The superior labial artery (superior labial branch of facial artery) is larger and more egregious than the inferior labial artery. It follows a similar course along the edge of the upper lip, lying between the mucous membrane and the orbicularis oris, and anastomoses with the artery of the opposite side.

superior_labial_vein_left.name: Superior labial vein (left)
superior_labial_vein_left.description: The superior labial vein is the vein receiving blood from the upper lip.

superior_labial_vein_right.name: Superior labial vein (right)
superior_labial_vein_right.description: The superior labial vein is the vein receiving blood from the upper lip.

superior_oblique_muscle_left.name: Superior oblique muscle (left)
superior_oblique_muscle_left.description: The superior oblique muscle, or obliquus oculi superior, is a fusiform muscle originating in the upper, medial side of the orbit (i.e. from beside the nose) which abducts, depresses and internally rotates the eye. It is the only extraocular muscle innervated by the trochlear nerve (the fourth cranial nerve).

superior_oblique_muscle_right.name: Superior oblique muscle (right)
superior_oblique_muscle_right.description: The superior oblique muscle, or obliquus oculi superior, is a fusiform muscle originating in the upper, medial side of the orbit (i.e. from beside the nose) which abducts, depresses and internally rotates the eye. It is the only extraocular muscle innervated by the trochlear nerve (the fourth cranial nerve).

superior_occipital_gyri_left.name: Superior occipital gyri (left)
superior_occipital_gyri_left.description: The occipital gyri (OcG) are three gyri in parallel, along the lateral portion of the occipital lobe, also referred to as a composite structure in the brain. The gyri are the superior occipital gyrus, the middle occipital gyrus, and the inferior occipital gyrus, and these are also known as the occipital face area.

superior_occipital_gyri_right.name: Superior occipital gyri (right)
superior_occipital_gyri_right.description: The occipital gyri (OcG) are three gyri in parallel, along the lateral portion of the occipital lobe, also referred to as a composite structure in the brain. The gyri are the superior occipital gyrus, the middle occipital gyrus, and the inferior occipital gyrus, and these are also known as the occipital face area.

superior_ophthalmic_vein_left.name: Superior ophthalmic vein (left)
superior_ophthalmic_vein_left.description: The superior ophthalmic vein is a vein of the orbit around the eye. It begins from the angular vein and the supraorbital vein, and passes through the superior orbital fissure to drain into the cavernous sinus.

superior_ophthalmic_vein_right.name: Superior ophthalmic vein (right)
superior_ophthalmic_vein_right.description: The superior ophthalmic vein is a vein of the orbit around the eye. It begins from the angular vein and the supraorbital vein, and passes through the superior orbital fissure to drain into the cavernous sinus.

superior_parietal_lobule_left.name: Superior parietal lobule (left)
superior_parietal_lobule_left.description: The superior parietal lobule is bounded in front by the upper part of the postcentral sulcus, but is usually connected with the postcentral gyrus above the end of the sulcus. The superior parietal lobule contains Brodmann's areas 5 and 7.

superior_parietal_lobule_right.name: Superior parietal lobule (right)
superior_parietal_lobule_right.description: The superior parietal lobule is bounded in front by the upper part of the postcentral sulcus, but is usually connected with the postcentral gyrus above the end of the sulcus. The superior parietal lobule contains Brodmann's areas 5 and 7.

superior_petrosal_sinus_left.name: Superior petrosal sinus (left)
superior_petrosal_sinus_left.description: The superior petrosal sinus is one of the dural venous sinuses located beneath the brain. It receives blood from the cavernous sinus and passes backward and laterally to drain into the transverse sinus. The sinus receives superior petrosal veins, some cerebellar veins, some inferior cerebral veins, and veins from the tympanic cavity.

superior_petrosal_sinus_right.name: Superior petrosal sinus (right)
superior_petrosal_sinus_right.description: The superior petrosal sinus is one of the dural venous sinuses located beneath the brain. It receives blood from the cavernous sinus and passes backward and laterally to drain into the transverse sinus. The sinus receives superior petrosal veins, some cerebellar veins, some inferior cerebral veins, and veins from the tympanic cavity.

superior_pharyngeal_constrictor_left.name: Superior pharyngeal constrictor (left)
superior_pharyngeal_constrictor_left.description: The superior pharyngeal constrictor muscle is a muscle in the pharynx. It is the highest located muscle of the three pharyngeal constrictors. The muscle is a quadrilateral muscle, thinner and paler than the inferior pharyngeal constrictor muscle and middle pharyngeal constrictor muscle.

superior_pharyngeal_constrictor_right.name: Superior pharyngeal constrictor (right)
superior_pharyngeal_constrictor_right.description: The superior pharyngeal constrictor muscle is a muscle in the pharynx. It is the highest located muscle of the three pharyngeal constrictors. The muscle is a quadrilateral muscle, thinner and paler than the inferior pharyngeal constrictor muscle and middle pharyngeal constrictor muscle.

superior_rectus_muscle_left.name: Superior rectus muscle (left)
superior_rectus_muscle_left.description: The superior rectus muscle is a muscle in the orbit. It is one of the extraocular muscles. It is innervated by the superior division of the oculomotor nerve (III). In the primary position (looking straight ahead), its primary function is elevation, although it also contributes to intorsion and adduction.

superior_rectus_muscle_right.name: Superior rectus muscle (right)
superior_rectus_muscle_right.description: The superior rectus muscle is a muscle in the orbit. It is one of the extraocular muscles. It is innervated by the superior division of the oculomotor nerve (III). In the primary position (looking straight ahead), its primary function is elevation, although it also contributes to intorsion and adduction.

superior_sagittal_sinus.name: Superior sagittal sinus
superior_sagittal_sinus.description: The superior sagittal sinus (also known as the superior longitudinal sinus), within the human head, is an unpaired area along the attached margin of the falx cerebri. It allows blood to drain from the lateral aspects of anterior cerebral hemispheres to the confluence of sinuses.

superior_salivatory_nucleus_left.name: Superior salivatory nucleus (left)
superior_salivatory_nucleus_left.description: The salivatory nuclei are the superior salivatory nucleus, and the inferior salivatory nucleus that innervate the salivary glands. They are located in the pontine tegmentum in the brainstem. They both are examples of cranial nerve nuclei.

superior_salivatory_nucleus_right.name: Superior salivatory nucleus (right)
superior_salivatory_nucleus_right.description: The salivatory nuclei are the superior salivatory nucleus, and the inferior salivatory nucleus that innervate the salivary glands. They are located in the pontine tegmentum in the brainstem. They both are examples of cranial nerve nuclei.

superior_tarsus_left.name: Superior tarsus (left)
superior_tarsus_left.description: The tarsi (tarsal plates) are two comparatively thick, elongated plates of dense connective tissue, about 10 mm (0.39 in) in length for the upper eyelid and 5 mm for the lower eyelid; one is found in each eyelid, and contributes to its form and support. They are located directly above the lid margins.

superior_tarsus_right.name: Superior tarsus (right)
superior_tarsus_right.description: The tarsi (tarsal plates) are two comparatively thick, elongated plates of dense connective tissue, about 10 mm (0.39 in) in length for the upper eyelid and 5 mm for the lower eyelid; one is found in each eyelid, and contributes to its form and support. They are located directly above the lid margins.

superior_temporal_gyrus_lateral_part_lef.name: Superior temporal gyrus (Lateral part) (left)
superior_temporal_gyrus_lateral_part_lef.description: The superior temporal gyrus (STG) is one of three (sometimes two) gyri in the temporal lobe of the human brain, which is located laterally to the head, situated somewhat above the external ear.

superior_temporal_gyrus_lateral_part_rig.name: Superior temporal gyrus (Lateral part) (right)
superior_temporal_gyrus_lateral_part_rig.description: The superior temporal gyrus (STG) is one of three (sometimes two) gyri in the temporal lobe of the human brain, which is located laterally to the head, situated somewhat above the external ear.

superior_temporal_sulcus_left.name: Superior temporal sulcus (left)
superior_temporal_sulcus_left.description: The superior temporal sulcus (STS) is the sulcus separating the superior temporal gyrus from the middle temporal gyrus in the temporal lobe of the brain. A sulcus (plural sulci) is a deep groove that curves into the largest part of the brain, the cerebrum, and a gyrus (plural gyri) is a ridge that curves outward of the cerebrum.

superior_temporal_sulcus_right.name: Superior temporal sulcus (right)
superior_temporal_sulcus_right.description: The superior temporal sulcus (STS) is the sulcus separating the superior temporal gyrus from the middle temporal gyrus in the temporal lobe of the brain. A sulcus (plural sulci) is a deep groove that curves into the largest part of the brain, the cerebrum, and a gyrus (plural gyri) is a ridge that curves outward of the cerebrum.

supramarginal_gyrus_left.name: Supramarginal gyrus (left)
supramarginal_gyrus_left.description: The supramarginal gyrus is a portion of the parietal lobe. This area of the brain is also known as Brodmann area 40 based on the brain map created by Korbinian Brodmann to define the structures in the cerebral cortex. It is probably involved with language perception and processing, and lesions in it may cause receptive aphasia.

supramarginal_gyrus_right.name: Supramarginal gyrus (right)
supramarginal_gyrus_right.description: The supramarginal gyrus is a portion of the parietal lobe. This area of the brain is also known as Brodmann area 40 based on the brain map created by Korbinian Brodmann to define the structures in the cerebral cortex. It is probably involved with language perception and processing, and lesions in it may cause receptive aphasia.

supratrochlear_artery_left.name: Supratrochlear artery (left)
supratrochlear_artery_left.description: The supratrochlear artery (or frontal artery) is one of the terminal branches of the ophthalmic artery. It branches from the ophthalmic artery near the trochlea of the superior oblique muscle in the orbit.

supratrochlear_artery_right.name: Supratrochlear artery (right)
supratrochlear_artery_right.description: The supratrochlear artery (or frontal artery) is one of the terminal branches of the ophthalmic artery. It branches from the ophthalmic artery near the trochlea of the superior oblique muscle in the orbit.

suspensory_ligament_of_eyeball_left.name: Suspensory ligament of eyeball (left)
suspensory_ligament_of_eyeball_left.description: The suspensory ligament of eyeball (or Lockwood's ligament) forms a hammock stretching below the eyeball between the medial and lateral check ligaments and enclosing the inferior rectus and inferior oblique muscles of the eye.

suspensory_ligament_of_eyeball_right.name: Suspensory ligament of eyeball (right)
suspensory_ligament_of_eyeball_right.description: The suspensory ligament of eyeball (or Lockwood's ligament) forms a hammock stretching below the eyeball between the medial and lateral check ligaments and enclosing the inferior rectus and inferior oblique muscles of the eye.

temporal_bone_left.name: Temporal bone (left)
temporal_bone_left.description: The temporal bones are situated at the sides and base of the skull, and lateral to the temporal lobes of the cerebral cortex. The temporal bones are overlaid by the sides of the head known as the temples, and house the structures of the ears.

temporal_bone_right.name: Temporal bone (right)
temporal_bone_right.description: The temporal bones are situated at the sides and base of the skull, and lateral to the temporal lobes of the cerebral cortex. The temporal bones are overlaid by the sides of the head known as the temples, and house the structures of the ears.

temporal_branches_of_middle_cerebral_art.name: Temporal branches of middle cerebral artery (left)
Temporal branches of middle cerebral artery (right)

temporal_plane_left.name: Temporal plane (left)
temporal_plane_left.description: The superior temporal gyrus (STG) is one of three (sometimes two) gyri in the temporal lobe of the human brain, which is located laterally to the head, situated somewhat above the external ear.

temporal_plane_right.name: Temporal plane (right)
temporal_plane_right.description: The superior temporal gyrus (STG) is one of three (sometimes two) gyri in the temporal lobe of the human brain, which is located laterally to the head, situated somewhat above the external ear.

temporal_pole_left.name: Temporal pole (left)
temporal_pole_left.description: There are three known poles of the cerebral hemispheres: the occipital pole, the frontal pole, and the temporal pole.

temporal_pole_right.name: Temporal pole (right)
temporal_pole_right.description: There are three known poles of the cerebral hemispheres: the occipital pole, the frontal pole, and the temporal pole.

temporal_region_left.name: Temporal region (left)
temporal_region_left.description: Above and around the ear. See: Temple

temporal_region_right.name: Temporal region (right)
temporal_region_right.description: Above and around the ear. See: Temple

temporalis_muscle_left.name: Temporalis muscle (left)
temporalis_muscle_left.description: In anatomy, the temporal muscle, also known as the temporalis, is one of the muscles of mastication. It is a broad, fan-shaped convergent muscle on each side of the head that fills the temporal fossa, superior to the zygomatic arch so it covers much of the temporal bone.Temporal refers to the head's temples.

temporalis_muscle_right.name: Temporalis muscle (right)
temporalis_muscle_right.description: In anatomy, the temporal muscle, also known as the temporalis, is one of the muscles of mastication. It is a broad, fan-shaped convergent muscle on each side of the head that fills the temporal fossa, superior to the zygomatic arch so it covers much of the temporal bone.Temporal refers to the head's temples.

temporoparietalis_muscle_left.name: Temporoparietalis muscle (left)
temporoparietalis_muscle_left.description: The temporoparietalis muscle is a distinct muscle of the head. It lies above the auricularis superior muscle. It lies just inferior to the epicranial aponeurosis of the occipitofrontalis muscle. The temporoparietalis muscle may be used in reconstructive ear surgery. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temporoparietalis_muscle

temporoparietalis_muscle_right.name: Temporoparietalis muscle (right)
temporoparietalis_muscle_right.description: The temporoparietalis muscle is a distinct muscle of the head. It lies above the auricularis superior muscle. It lies just inferior to the epicranial aponeurosis of the occipitofrontalis muscle. The temporoparietalis muscle may be used in reconstructive ear surgery. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temporoparietalis_muscle

tentorium_cerebelli_left.name: Tentorium cerebelli (left)
tentorium_cerebelli_left.description: The cerebellar tentorium or tentorium cerebelli (Latin for "tent of the cerebellum") is an extension of the dura mater that separates the cerebellum from the inferior portion of the occipital lobes.

tentorium_cerebelli_right.name: Tentorium cerebelli (right)
tentorium_cerebelli_right.description: The cerebellar tentorium or tentorium cerebelli (Latin for "tent of the cerebellum") is an extension of the dura mater that separates the cerebellum from the inferior portion of the occipital lobes.

thalamus_left.name: Thalamus (left)
thalamus_left.description: The thalamus (from Greek θάλαμος, "chamber") is a large mass of gray matter located in the dorsal part of the diencephalon (a division of the forebrain). Nerve fibers project out of the thalamus to the cerebral cortex in all directions, allowing hub-like exchanges of information.

thalamus_right.name: Thalamus (right)
thalamus_right.description: The thalamus (from Greek θάλαμος, "chamber") is a large mass of gray matter located in the dorsal part of the diencephalon (a division of the forebrain). Nerve fibers project out of the thalamus to the cerebral cortex in all directions, allowing hub-like exchanges of information.

third_ventricle.name: Third ventricle
third_ventricle.description: The third ventricle is one of the four connected ventricles of the ventricular system within the mammalian brain.

thyro_epiglottic_part_of_thyro_arytenoid.name: Thyro-epiglottic part of thyro-arytenoid muscle (left)
thyro_epiglottic_part_of_thyro_arytenoid.description: Origin: In front, on the internal surface of the thyroid cartilage. Insertion: epiglottis and quadrangular membrane. Innervation: recurrent laryngeal nerve.

thyro_epiglottic_part_of_thyro_arytenoid.name: Thyro-epiglottic part of thyro-arytenoid muscle (right)
thyro_epiglottic_part_of_thyro_arytenoid.description: Origin: In front, on the internal surface of the thyroid cartilage. Insertion: epiglottis and quadrangular membrane. Innervation: recurrent laryngeal nerve.

thyrohyoid_muscle_left.name: Thyrohyoid muscle (left)
thyrohyoid_muscle_left.description: The thyrohyoid muscle is a small skeletal muscle on the neck. It originates from the lamina of the thyroid cartilage, and inserts into the greater cornu of the hyoid bone. It is supplied by the hypoglossal nerve, and a branch of the ventral rami of the cervical plexus, spinal nerve C1, which travels with the hypoglossal nerve.

thyrohyoid_muscle_right.name: Thyrohyoid muscle (right)
thyrohyoid_muscle_right.description: The thyrohyoid muscle is a small skeletal muscle on the neck. It originates from the lamina of the thyroid cartilage, and inserts into the greater cornu of the hyoid bone. It is supplied by the hypoglossal nerve, and a branch of the ventral rami of the cervical plexus, spinal nerve C1, which travels with the hypoglossal nerve.

tongue.name: Tongue
tongue.description: The tongue is a muscular organ in the mouth of a typical tetrapod. It manipulates food for mastication and swallowing as part of the digestive process, and is the primary organ of taste. The tongue's upper surface (dorsum) is covered by taste buds housed in numerous lingual papillae.

tragus_left.name: Tragus (left)
tragus_left.description: The tragus is a small pointed eminence of the external ear, situated in front of the concha, and projecting backward over the meatus. It also is the name of hair growing at the entrance of the ear.

tragus_right.name: Tragus (right)
tragus_right.description: The tragus is a small pointed eminence of the external ear, situated in front of the concha, and projecting backward over the meatus. It also is the name of hair growing at the entrance of the ear.

transverse_facial_artery_left.name: Transverse facial artery (left)
transverse_facial_artery_left.description: The transverse facial artery is an artery that branches from the superficial temporal artery and runs across the face.

transverse_facial_artery_right.name: Transverse facial artery (right)
transverse_facial_artery_right.description: The transverse facial artery is an artery that branches from the superficial temporal artery and runs across the face.

transverse_occipital_sulcus_left.name: Transverse occipital sulcus (left)
transverse_occipital_sulcus_left.description: The transverse occipital sulcus is a structure in the occipital lobe. The transverse occipital sulcus is continuous with the posterior end of the occipital ramus of the intraparietal sulcus, and runs across the upper part of the lobe, a short distance behind the parietooccipital fissure.

transverse_occipital_sulcus_right.name: Transverse occipital sulcus (right)
transverse_occipital_sulcus_right.description: The transverse occipital sulcus is a structure in the occipital lobe. The transverse occipital sulcus is continuous with the posterior end of the occipital ramus of the intraparietal sulcus, and runs across the upper part of the lobe, a short distance behind the parietooccipital fissure.

transverse_sinus_left.name: Transverse sinus (left)
transverse_sinus_left.description: The transverse sinuses (left and right lateral sinuses), within the human head, are two areas beneath the brain which allow blood to drain from the back of the head. They run laterally in a groove along the interior surface of the occipital bone.

transverse_sinus_right.name: Transverse sinus (right)
transverse_sinus_right.description: The transverse sinuses (left and right lateral sinuses), within the human head, are two areas beneath the brain which allow blood to drain from the back of the head. They run laterally in a groove along the interior surface of the occipital bone.

transverse_temporal_gyri_left.name: Transverse temporal gyri (left)
transverse_temporal_gyri_left.description: The transverse temporal gyri, also called Heschl's gyri () or Heschl's convolutions, are gyri found in the area of primary auditory cortex buried within the lateral sulcus of the human brain, occupying Brodmann areas 41 and 42.

transverse_temporal_gyri_right.name: Transverse temporal gyri (right)
transverse_temporal_gyri_right.description: The transverse temporal gyri, also called Heschl's gyri () or Heschl's convolutions, are gyri found in the area of primary auditory cortex buried within the lateral sulcus of the human brain, occupying Brodmann areas 41 and 42.

triangular_fossa_left.name: Triangular fossa (left)
triangular_fossa_left.description: Antero-superior depression between the two branches of the antihelix (crura of antihelix).

triangular_fossa_right.name: Triangular fossa (right)
triangular_fossa_right.description: Antero-superior depression between the two branches of the antihelix (crura of antihelix).

triangular_part_of_inferior_frontal_gyru.name: Triangular part of inferior frontal gyrus (left)
triangular_part_of_inferior_frontal_gyru.description: Triangular part of inferior frontal gyrus (pars triangularis), (cortex between the ascending ramus and the horizontal ramus of the lateral sulcus). It may be associated with the ability to translate from a secondary or tertiary language back to one's native language.

triangular_part_of_inferior_frontal_gyru.name: Triangular part of inferior frontal gyrus (right)
triangular_part_of_inferior_frontal_gyru.description: Triangular part of inferior frontal gyrus (pars triangularis), (cortex between the ascending ramus and the horizontal ramus of the lateral sulcus). It may be associated with the ability to translate from a secondary or tertiary language back to one's native language.

trigeminal_nerve_v_left.name: Trigeminal nerve (V) (left)
trigeminal_nerve_v_left.description: The trigeminal nerve (the fifth cranial nerve, or simply CN V) is a nerve responsible for sensation in the face and motor functions such as biting and chewing; it is the most complex of the cranial nerves.

trigeminal_nerve_v_right.name: Trigeminal nerve (V) (right)
trigeminal_nerve_v_right.description: The trigeminal nerve (the fifth cranial nerve, or simply CN V) is a nerve responsible for sensation in the face and motor functions such as biting and chewing; it is the most complex of the cranial nerves.

trochlea_of_superior_oblique_muscle_left.name: Trochlea of superior oblique muscle (left)
trochlea_of_superior_oblique_muscle_left.description: The superior oblique muscle loops through a pulley-like structure (the trochlea of superior oblique) and inserts into the sclera on the posterotemporal surface of the eyeball. It is the pulley system that gives superior oblique its actions, causing depression of the eyeball despite being inserted on the superior surface.

trochlea_of_superior_oblique_muscle_righ.name: Trochlea of superior oblique muscle (right)
trochlea_of_superior_oblique_muscle_righ.description: The superior oblique muscle loops through a pulley-like structure (the trochlea of superior oblique) and inserts into the sclera on the posterotemporal surface of the eyeball. It is the pulley system that gives superior oblique its actions, causing depression of the eyeball despite being inserted on the superior surface.

trochlear_nerve_iv_left.name: Trochlear nerve (IV) (left)
trochlear_nerve_iv_left.description: The trochlear nerve (), also called the fourth cranial nerve or CN IV, is a motor nerve (a somatic efferent nerve) that innervates just one muscle: the superior oblique muscle of the eye, which operates through the pulley-like trochlea.

trochlear_nerve_iv_right.name: Trochlear nerve (IV) (right)
